Minister): I should like to lay on the table a copy of the order in council with respect to the authorization of an insurance policy for the purchase of wheat by the Polish government. The decision had been made on June 15, 1955.
The hon. member had asked me to ascertain the exact date. The formal order in council was passed only yesterday. There had to be details ascertained; but the decision had been made, and hon. members will know that frequently decisions are made by cabinet with instructions that an order in council be prepared and passed. There is, I would not like to call it a routine committee, but I shall call it a small committee of the cabinet which meets more frequently than the whole committee, and it had a meeting yesterday afternoon and passed the order in council which I am now tabling.

maintopic: ALLEGED DELAY IN BRINGING DOWN RETURNS TO ORDERS
subtopic: REPLY BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have had searches made with respect to the remarks yesterday of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) about returns. I must say I was rather surprised at his statement that there was a return due since December of 1953. I have ascertained that after that order was made the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) wrote a letter to the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker), the mover, explaining to him the, while not absolute objections, reasons suggested by the government of the United States that it would not be desirable to have that correspondence published and available


to the press, and sending copies for the personal information of the hon. member. He acknowledged receipt of the copies sent to him and said that he would discuss it with the Secretary of State for External Affairs; and it just remained in that position. So that is the explanation for that item.
The next is a return ordered on February 9 for the correspondence in connection with the purchase of lumber and building materials required by the department of Indian affairs in Prince Albert and northern Saskatchewan. There were several very voluminous files, and the minister wrote on March 3, 1955, to the hon. member giving him a list of the contracts that had been made, and asking him if he required the correspondence with respect to all the contracts, or if there were one or more in which he was particularly interested. It has remained in that position since that time.
An order was made on March 9, on the motion of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), requesting the correspondence between the federal government and the provincial governments relating to the calling of the federal-provincial conference. The return was prepared. Letters were written to all the provincial premiers concerned on April 1, asking for their acquiescence in the tabling of this correspondence. Answers were received from all but the premier of Ontario. A follow-up letter was written to him on June 17, reminding him that there had been no answer to-the letter of April 1, and that letter of June 17 has not yet been answered. The return has been ready, but we were waiting for the answer.
There was a return ordered on April 25, on motion of the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny), concerning court orders obtained by the Department of National Revenue for the payment of income tax. This requires work that was put in hand immediately the order was made, but has not yet been completed.
There was an address on that same day on the motion of the hon. member for Prince Albert requesting correspondence between the government and the Kerr-Gifford and Company concerning an elevator at Ballan-tyne pier, Vancouver. The papers, I understand, were received in the office of the Secretary of State yesterday, and the return will be tabled probably on Monday. There are other orders that were made, and they are now in the office of the privy council where they are being checked. They will be tabled just as soon as the accuracy can be certified.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the Prime Minister tor the information regarding these orders. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Prime Minister, notice of which I sent him about half an hour ago, and which he may take as notice if he so desires. speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROTEST DELAY IN CONSTRUCTION OF ALL-CANADIAN PIPE LINE

Mr. Speaker, a telegram was received which came to my attention on Wednesday, 6th of July, and was referred to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and of which an acknowledgment was sent to the two mayors of Fort William and Port Arthur. Now the hon. gentleman suggests that I bring the house up to date. That would be quite difficult.
There are three alternatives that are being very carefully investigated and about which, of course, the commitments of many different interests are required. There is one that we prefer to the other two. There is a third that we do not like as well even as the second. The officials of the Canadian company are endeavouring to get the commitments that would provide for the implementing of No. 1. They are also ascertaining whether, in the event that is not possible, they could get the commitments that would be necessary for the implementation of No. 2. That is the situation. I hope we shall not have to fall back on No. 3.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: the third reading of Bill No. 506, to amend the Customs Tariff.

Mr. Speaker, I merely wish to reiterate a request I made when the bill received second reading. The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance was handling the bill at that time, and I now make the request to the minister. I merely reiterate the request that reconsideration and study be given during the next year to that curious item in the act having to do with the restoration of the coal drawback notwithstanding that there is no longer any duty on coal, and which was done ias an indirect way of authorizing the bounty payable on coke used in the manufacture of steel. In my opinion this is a very indirect and almost grotesque way of achieving the desired result.

On June 29 when this bill was in committee, I raised the question of the increase in the tariff on ethylene glycol. I am not going to hold the house very long, but I wish to say that any increase in tariff which results in an increase in the cost of production of agricultural products will be opposed by myself and my colleagues. In my opinion, the proposal of the government to increase the customs duty on ethylene glycol, which goes into the manufacture of antifreeze, will result in a higher cost of production on the farms. It will result also, in my opinion, in a higher cost to consumers generally of antifreeze, a commodity which is very widely used in Canada and which is practically an essential commodity.
When this question was being heard by the tariff board, representations were made in favour of the increase by two companies, both of which are interested in the manufacture of this commodity in Canada and both of which are subsidiaries of parent companies in the United States. These two companies are in a very good position to form a virtual monopoly in the sale of that product in Canada. With this added protection, they have that much more opportunity to set up that kind of monopoly. As a matter of fact, it was the opinion of one of the representatives of the processing company that uses the raw material, ethylene glycol, to turn it into antifreeze that the placing of a higher tariff on glycol from the United States would result in the setting up of a

Customs Tariff
monopoly on that product in Canada. It was stated also by a representative of one of the two companies requesting the increase that their objective was the whole Canadian market, and that was their reason for asking for this protection.
The proposal to raise the tariff was opposed by the interprovincial farm union council. It was opposed to the extent that it would increase prices for antifreeze in Canada by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. As I have already mentioned, it was opposed by the representative of one of the processing companies which turns the raw product into antifreeze.
In defence of what I was saying on that occasion, the assistant to the Minister of Finance stated that what was represented in this bill was a rearrangement of certain budget items. Now, to a certain extent that is so. There has been a rearrangement, and I acknowledge that there has been, in another item, a net decrease of 5 per cent on the finished product, the antifreeze, but the fact still remains in spite of any claim of rearrangement and in spite of the fact that this was done by negotiation under GATT, that part of the ethylene glycol which was on the free list, in other words that part which was 97 per cent pure and not a mixture and which had free entry into Canada since about 1939, is now going to be subject to a 10 per cent tariff from the United States and of course a 25 per cent general tariff.
The other defence that was made by the minister's assistant was that the government does not go as far in proposing this increase as the two chemical companies had requested. Now, that also is true. If the two chemical companies asking for this protection had got what they wanted, it would have amounted to approximately 45 per cent or thereabouts, depending on the price of the commodity at the time. In my opinion, that is not an excuse for doing something which is not desirable so far as the Canadian economy is concerned. I have already pointed out that the two companies requesting the increase stated as their objective, and the reason for the increase, the obtaining of the whole Canadian market for ethylene glycol. The only reason that they could want the whole Canadian market would be to command higher prices. If the base product commands a higher price then the finished product, which is antifreeze, will also command a higher price and to that extent will enter into the cost of production of agricultural products particularly and increased prices to the consumers of those products.

In view of all these reasons I should like to move at this time, seconded by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce):
That Bill No. 506 be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole house for the purpose of reconsidering tariff item 207c as set out in schedule B to the said bill.
Perhaps I should make it clear when I refer to the reconsideration of this tariff item I mean that I am in favour of placing this product that goes into the manufacture of antifreeze on the free list. If this motion carries and the bill is referred back to the committee of the whole house, we will be prepared to present further arguments as to why this should be done.

If there is no one else who desires to speak on this matter at once, I should like to support this measure. There is no reason why we should have a tariff on any commodity coming into Canada to prevent it from competing with Canadian goods. We can subsidize Canadian goods so far as is necessary to enable them to take the Canadian market. We could use a quota to shut out external goods which we do not desire to have come into the Canadian market. By these means, we could effectively exclude all products of any kind whatever from the Canadian market, so long as they are undesirable to us in the Canadian market, without any resulting increase in price. Therefore, I support the hon. member's motion.

I was	paired with the hon.
member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Goode).

Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to point out all the members who did not vote on this measure which is interesting to the west. I want to point out that it is possible to manage the economy of Canada in such a way that a subsidy such as I spoke in favour of a few minutes ago-

Very well. I will talk
about the measure before the house now. I am leading up to that, anyway.
As matters stand today, an ordinary member of the Liberal party, and an ordinary member of the Conservative party, would say they could not favour the granting of a subsidy on a Canadian product to bring down the price low enough to enable it to compete successfully with goods coming in from outside. They would say they could not support that measure because it would cost the consolidated revenue fund money; it would cost the taxpayers money. Oh, oh.

Of course, there will be superficial laughs from those who do not know. Let me point out this important fact, that in 1933 and 1934 the people of Japan used her national credit in such a way that they were able to subsidize the exports of their goods to such an extent that they were able to compete successfully with similar goods produced in Britain and put the manufacturers of those goods entirely out of business.
Now, if they could do that successfully in exporting goods, they could certainly have subsidized the price of their own goods in Japan to render it impossible for any goods we might send to Japan to compete successfully with their goods. It was the use of the national credit which was made in that respect. Japan increased her external trade, in 1933 and 1934, 53 per cent. She was the only nation in the world that increased her trade during those years. How was she able to do it? Because she used her national credit. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, what I desire to point out is this. The wise use of the national credit of Canada would enable us to avoid the tremendous cost to Canada of

Supply-Justice
goods made in Canada which we force upon our people because we desire to protect our own producers in Canada. Consequently, I rejoice that I voted against this bill, and we intend to vote against the bill now and all similar bills. The time is coming when we in Canada have simply got to learn realities about finance, and not go on trying to finance our affairs in the silly, old, useless, outmoded financial way that intelligent men stopped trying to use 40 years ago.

DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE Royal Canadian Mounted police-
409. Administration, operation and maintenance, $6,992,087.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I understand that
this morning we are to deal with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, resolution 409, to be found on page 62 of the main estimates. The details start on page 507.

Mr. Chairman, earlier this week I asked the government and the Minister of Justice whether they would reconsider the demand which has been made upon the municipalities in British Columbia, which have their police services provided by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police under contract, for an increase in payment under that contract. This request comes, as I understand it, from four municipalities affected, including the city of Kamloops, which of course is the one from which I have had direct representation.
On June 3 of this year I was asked by the council of the corporation of the city of Kamloops to take up with the government the protest made by that municipal corporation against this increase, in the following terms. This is a resolution of the council of the city of Kamloops, passed on June 1, 1955:
That we register a strong protest against the action taken by the federal government in connection with the renewal of contracts with cities and municipalities for policing services for the following reasons:
1. The decision of the federal government to increase the per capita cost of the R.C.M.P. force came too late to enable municipalities to make provision for the increase in cost in their current budgets.
[Mr. Blackmore.l
2. The decision of the federal government to charge a larger percentage of the per capita cost of the R.C.M.P. force to municipalities having a population of 5000 or more, commencing with the period of June 1, 1957, will result in discrimination against larger centres, and further that we urge the provincial government to protest the action of the federal government on this matter and request that the provisions of the last agreement be continued to January 1, 1956.
It will be appreciated that the resolution indicates objection to the action of the government in this respect on two grounds. I should like to deal at this stage mainly with the first of those grounds, namely that the decision to increase the charge to the municipalities on a per capita basis of the number of men involved came too late for those municipalities to make provision in their current budgets. Yesterday in answer to a question on the orders of the day the minister told us that as he recalled it the decision was made on April 4. I do not know the actual date when that decision was communicated to the city of Kamloops, but I should imagine it was not long before June 3, the date of the letter which I received passing on the resolution which was dated June 1. Therefore I am not in a position to assess the responsibility, if there be any, for not getting this information to the municipalities concerned at an early date. But the fact is, as appears from the record, that they did not get it in time. If someone other than the federal government is responsible I imagine that the minister will make it clear to us just who it is.
These municipalities have their budgets set and approved by the council and have struck their tax rates accordingly. A municipality under our municipal act cannot run around and change the tax rate after it has once been approved. They do not have anything in the way of supplementary estimates such as we have here. Once a city council has approved the budget and set the tax rate accordingly that is the situation for that year.
I am informed that the result of this will be that the cities will either have to borrow this money or else have a debt on their hands of the expected demand from the R.C.M.P. for an increase in the contract rate. Under these circumstances I ask the minister in all reasonableness to accept this suggestion made in the resolution on behalf of the municipality and not change the rate until January 1, 1956. Otherwise I just do not know what the municipalities can do about it because they have no way of raising revenue to pay this demand now being made of them.
The municipalities would rather not pay this at all, but I do not know whether they

have any option if the government decides to make the demand that they pay it. They probably will pay it in future, but I do think that they should be accommodated at least to the extent of continuing the present rate to the first of next year.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if I could say a few words before the minister replies following up the matter raised by the hon. member for Kamloops. The problem which the hon. member has outlined is of considerable concern to some of the cities on Vancouver island which have their police services supplied by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police under contract. As a matter of fact, according to press reports which have come to my attention, the matter has gone so far that the mayor of Port Alberni has considered withdrawing from the arrangement with the R.C.M.P. and setting up something in the way of a municipal police force. Personally I feel that that would be a regrettable step.
I consider that the co-ordination of police services which is possible on Vancouver island through the present arrangement has many advantages. The minister will recall that this was in effect prior to the absorption of the British Columbia provincial force into the R.C.M.P. I think that that arrangement has proved to have many advantages. While I am not familiar with all the details of the present contract arrangements it does appear to me that a large percentage of the work done by the R.C.M.P. is not concerned primarily with the municipal field. I would say that a good deal of it arises because of laws passed in this chamber and for that reason I do not think it is logical to expect the municipal authorities to raise taxes in order to pay an undue proportion of the costs of police services.
With respect to the other point raised by the hon. member for Kamloops, the date of the coming into force of this increase, may I say that I was not able to catch the exact date given yesterday by the minister but I believe it was in the month of April. That would be long past the closing date of financial arrangements in most of the municipalities. These municipalities enter into their budgeting discussions and financial arrangements for the current year shortly after the first of the year. I know that these matters occupy the attention of city councils in my area shortly after the municipal elections have taken place.
I feel that there is considerable merit in the suggestion put forward by the hon. member for Kamloops in respect to the additional 50133-8711
Supply-Justice
problem which is being created by these increased rates and their being put into force without adequate notification to the municipalities concerned.

Mr. Chairman, may I say just a word before the minister replies and perhaps draw his attention to another related matter, which he could answer at the same time. I appreciate the problem raised by the hon. member for Kamloops and the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. There are several municipalities in Alberta which find themselves in exactly the same position. They had budgeted for the year's expenses before the notice of the increase in the per capita cost of policing by the R.C.M.P. was received and as a consequence will find it most difficult to carry on this year without borrowing or resorting to some extraordinary means of financing. I think that the suggestion has been made that there could be a delay in giving effect to the increase until the beginning of the next fiscal year. These municipalities might very well entertain that.
In addition to that, there is another problem I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. One of the best things that municipalities and provinces have ever done in the police field was to engage the R.C.M.P. to police the municipalities and provinces. They have been an excellent force. They have done a splendid job. All the municipalities I know about that have had experience with that type of policing over the years have spoken in the highest terms of the efficiency of the service they have had from the R.C.M.P. Now they face the problem of not being able to obtain any further services. I am told that it is because the R.C.M.P. are having trouble getting young men of the kind required for an extension of the force. I do not know whether this is because of the fact that sufficient salaries are not being paid or that young men are not interested in the force. Perhaps the minister might let us have his views with respect to the problem.
I know that in my own constituency there are two or three municipalities that have recently made application for this service by the R.C.M.P. They have been notified that there can be no further extension of the service in the province until such time as more men have been recruited and trained ready for the job. They have also been told it has been very difficult in past months to get the kind of personnel required. I wonder if the minister could let us know what the situation is in that regard, and also let us know if it would be possible to delay putting into effect the increase in the cost of the

Supply-Justice
police force to the municipalities until at least the beginning of their next fiscal year.

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, perhaps I might first deal with the last question which has been asked by the hon. member for Peace River, that is to say, the question which had to do with the difficulty of getting the mounted police to take on new municipal contracts. There is no question about our continuing any of the existing contracts. Municipalities, seeing other municipalities having the advantage of the police contracts and wishing to secure that advantage themselves, apply to us and we have not been able, during an interval now, to take on these new contracts. Among the reasons for this condition is that, to begin with, we maintain an exceedingly high standard in the force, and I do not think there is any member of the house who would wish us to lower that.
We all agree on that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, we all agree on that.
We select only one out of approximately 13 applicants for admission to the force. That is to say, only one out of 13 measures up to the standard which we think should be maintained if the force is to maintain its very high morale and prestige.
At the beginning of this legislative session there was some discussion with regard to a possible recession in Canada and to some difficulty about unemployment; but our experience is that men of the type that we want in the force have not had the slightest difficulty in the Canadian economy in getting quite attractive positions. Whilst as hon. members know we have made a number of increases in the salaries of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and are now paying good wages, and while we have been able to maintain the membership at quite a high level, what is perhaps not sufficiently appreciated is the conditions in the world which necessitate, for example, our devoting quite a large number of the force to security work. These responsibilities make unavailable for the taking on of municipal contracts members of the force who might otherwise have been used for that purpose. As a result, we have not been able to accede to the requests of all the municipalities which have applied to us recently. But our personnel position is improving, and I am hopeful that in the fairly near future we may be able to re-examine our position in that regard.
With regard to the embarrassment which has arisen in connection with certain municipalities in British Columbia and Alberta, in that they are alleged-and I think quite correctly-not to have received information 
about these increases in their police contract costs before the time that they set their budgets and pass their rate by-laws, I would say that, so far as the federal government is concerned, we must completely disclaim any responsibility for that result. We knew what had to be done in this connection. We ascertained in advance that the information in relation to police costs would have to be in the possession of the municipalities by the 15th day of May.
As a matter of fact, Assistant Commissioner Carnac, the head of the mounted police in the province of British Columbia, was advised on February 8, 1955, by the department of municipal affairs that the municipal act of British Columbia required a municipal council to pass its rate by-law on or before the 15th day of May each year. We proceeded on that basis to reach a decision ourselves here on April 4, 1955, as I find upon examining the facts that I correctly informed my hon. friend from Kamloops the day before yesterday. That decision was immediately communicated to Assistant Commissioner Carnac; but because the attorney general of British Columbia was away at that time, he was not able to pass it on until 18th April to the attorney general of British Columbia, who desired to have that information go through him to the municipalities. But it was communicated on the 18th April. What happened after that date we do not know, but certainly it was through no fault of ours that the information was not in the hands of the municipalities before the 15th day of May. We provided it in plenty of time that it could have been there at that time.
In the case of Alberta, we notified the province of Alberta prior to April 28, and we were advised by the Alberta government that the approval of that government to this arrangement had been made on April 28. I presume the date on which the municipal by-law is to be passed in Alberta is about the same time as in British Columbia. So the information was there. Any arrangements as between the provincial government and the municipalities are peculiarly the responsibility of the provincial government. The municipalities are the creatures of the provincial government and under its direction of provincial statutes in most of the things they do.
When it is suggested that we should just forget about it for this year, I should like to point out that in the two years that have elapsed since our last adjustment of these contracts, at which time the per capita cost of the member of the force was established at $2,000, the cost has crept up from $2,000

to $2,360. With this time lag in our ability to pass on to the municipality the increased cost which we were immediately sustaining, it has meant that during that period of two years we have sustained a fairly substantial increase in cost which we have not been able to pass on. Therefore when the time comes that we can legally do so, and when we have taken the pains to find out and inform the municipalities as to what the amount is, and have taken every step at the appropriate time and passed the information on through the proper channels to the municipalities, I do not think I could possibly justify to my colleague, the Minister of Finance, that we should absorb more costs above our contract on top of those which the terms of the contract have required that we absorb during the past two years.
That is the reason why I said, when the hon. member for Kamloops asked me this question on the orders of the day, that we had gone very carefully into all the factors having to do with this contract and no additional circumstances had been brought forward which seemed to us to warrant our reconsideration of the decision which we had reached.

Under the circumstances outlined by the minister I think it is difficult to suggest that the responsibility for the situation in which the municipalities And themselves falls on him or the officials here, although I suggest, as did the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, that while April 18, which was when the attorney general of British Columbia got the information, is nearly a month in advance of the statutory deadline, it is probably the limit, if not actually the limit, so far as a practical deadline is concerned from the point of view of the date by which the municipalities have in fact set their tax rates. However, I do not suppose it would be profitable in any event to argue back and forth who was responsible for any delay in the information being received.
I accept the facts as the minister has stated them. However, because the situation is obviously not the responsibility of the municipalities and is something about which they can do absolutely nothing, I had hoped that the government would consider deferring the effective date of the increase until January 1, 1956. I will not give up hope that the minister will still see his way clear to do it.
I should like, however, to suggest another alternative, and I want to make it clear that I have no authority to do so. I have not been instructed by the council of the city of Kamloops, nor do I know that there are any
Supply-Justice
other city councils which have made this suggestion. However, it occurs to me that the department might say: Well, all right, we will not insist upon payment of that this year, but in 1956 we will expect you to pay what will then be the going rate and what will amount to arrears on the current contract. As I say, I do not know whether or not that would be satisfactory to the municipalities. I imagine it would be a little better than having to scrape it up from somewhere, heaven knows where, this year. In setting their tax rates for next year they would have to make up the arrears for this year.
As I say, I hope the minister will still see his way clear to say that because of the situation, which is none of your responsibility even as it is none of ours, we will forgo it for this year, but if he cannot do that then I think he should ask if it would be helpful to the municipalities to allow the contract for this year to be in arrears by agreement, with the arrears to be made up next year.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In all these arrangements that we have with the provinces and the municipalities we have to be as co-operative as we can. They will not work unless we keep on a friendly basis with the other parties to the contracts. Therefore in all these contracts we have for policing with provincial governments and with municipalities we try to be as co-operative and as easy to deal with as we possibly can be; for it is only by there being a satisfactory mutual feeling that the full benefits of an arrangement of this sort can be realized. Therefore, while we have not received any such proposal as that made by the hon. member for Kamloops, if we did receive one I would think I would be quite warranted in seeing whether the Department of Finance and the treasury board would be willing to consider it. It would really be for them to consider. We would not actually lose money under such an arrangement. There would just be a delay. I think that is what my hon. friend has in mind.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: But I share his doubts whether that would be very satisfactory even from the standpoint of the municipalities because it would mean that next year they would have the two annual police levies to take care of in their tax rates.

Would the minister tell the committee the procedure by which these contracts are entered into with municipalities? Is application made by the municipality through the attorney general's department of the province and is payment made on the

Supply-Justice
contract by the municipality through the provincial government or directly to the Department of Justice?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The answer to my hon. friend's first question is that some of the contracts are made through the provincial government and some of them are made directly. We do not stand on ceremony. If they want to apply directly we will deal with them. On the other hand, if they want to apply the other way we will accommodate them that way. When the contract has been made, however, payments are made directly by the municipality to us.

I feel the same way about this matter&as the hon. member for Kamloops and the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, especially on the question of replacing the R.C.M.P. by local police forces. I am in an area bordering on the United States, and the minister appreciates the difficulty we have had on the lower mainland of British Columbia so far as narcotics are concerned. We could have a very dangerous condition existing again. We have the mounted policemen at the border looking after that particular problem and the fact that we have them throughout the whole of the riding has assisted a great deal, I am sure, in preventing the carrying on of the narcotic traffic in that region.
With respect to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Kamloops concerning leaving the payment of arrears until next year, I feel very much as the minister does. If a municipality cannot keep up its payments it probably will not be able to catch up on arrears. However, if municipalities are desirous of doing that perhaps the minister could pass on their requests to the Minister of Finance. It would be the responsibility of the particular municipality and it would be up to them to decide what they wanted to do.
There is one other point that should be considered. I refer to the fact that our mounted policemen cost a considerable sum of money to train. I realize their training is of such a nature that they are specialists in their own field. Many municipalities use them as traffic policemen. Practically anyone can be trained to be a traffic policeman. If these municipalities could find other means of looking after the traffic problem in their own areas and free the mounted police to do the work they are trained to do more particularly, I think we would then have an efficient police force. The municipalities might be able to cut down on the number of mounted police they need and yet the same service could be rendered as is being rendered today.
Does the minister wish to answer now, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, I think I might briefly answer the special point which the hon. member who has just taken his seat has raised before we go on to another item. So far as the mounted police are concerned, they agree that it is undesirable to use a man who has had the special training of a mounted policeman in town traffic work and checking parking. We would be quite receptive to any suggestion that such work might be done by some officer of the municipality who is not a member of the mounted police.

I would appreciate it if the minister would give us some information upon the other aspect of this problem which confronts municipalities by way of a demand for an increased payment. As I understand it, there is firstly a demand for an increased per capita payment and secondly, that municipalities over 5,000 population have to pay a bigger proportion of the per capita costs than those with less than 5,000 population. I wonder if the minister would say a word on that, as to why these municipalities of over 5,000 should be discriminated against. I am unable to see why a municipality of say 6,000 would have that much more strictly local work to do than a municipality of say 4,990, to justify their having to pay more for the services of the mounted police than other municipalities.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, I think that the most satisfactory and comprehensive way of replying to the point which the hon. member for Kamloops has raised is for me to paraphrase the text of a letter which I sent recently to the editor of the Vancouver Province in response to an editorial which he wrote demanding, as he had a right to do as a representative of a free press, an explanation as to why these costs had been increased. In so doing I am really stating my own views as set out in this letter.
First, I should like to make it clear that there has been no change in the basis for the rate charged, though there has been an increase in the amount. Throughout the years, the charges to the cities and towns per member of the police employed has been roughly 40 per cent of the operating costs per member. The amount represented by this 40 per cent has, I think quite understandably, gone up as operating costs go up. There has been a big rise in the operating costs since 1949, and the pay alone has increased some 40 per cent in that interval. The present pay rate is reasonable, but not extravagant. I think that most of the members would agree with me in this. I believe, for example, that was implicit in the remarks that were made by the hon. member for Peace River, that had the government not made an upward

adjustment in line with the general wage and salary scales we certainly would not have been able to keep the force up to strength with the calibre of men needed. Indeed, the fact we have not sufficient strength in order to take on new contracts is proof, if proof were needed, that that is so.
The present contract rate is based upon 40 per cent of the per capita cost, as it has been throughout. This is the point the hon. member for Kamloops has now raised. It is true that we propose to increase this rate in 1957-not now but in 1957-to 50 per cent in small towns and to 75 per cent in the larger cities and towns employing over five men. Notice to this effect has been given now so that the municipal government may have ample opportunity to consider what is involved. These rates will apply in all provinces as the old ones did. At that time, that is in 1957, cities and towns in British Columbia will have had the services of the force at the rate originally negotiated, that is 40 per cent of the per capita cost, for a period of over six years.
Our 1950 contract with the province of British Columbia was for a period of five years. Bearing all these things in mind, I do not think it could be suggested that when the force has become entrenched in British Columbia we then sought to raise its rates arbitrarily. That was a suggestion that was made in this editorial, that we got our foot in the door, established ourselves and the need for our force, and then we hoisted the rates arbitrarily. In writing this letter, I did not overlook the fact that cities and towns supply certain other services and pay for car mileage over and above the first 3,100 miles, in addition to the basic charges per man. On the other hand, I think that it would be fair to point out that the amount being charged the municipalities by the British Columbia provincial police just prior to the disbandment of that force in 1950 was $2,663.69 per man per annum. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police took over the British Columbia provincial police commitment and collected payment in the same amount, $2,663.69 per man per annum for the last five months of 1950, then entered into new contracts direct with British Columbia municipalities at the same $1,400 rate as then applied in other provinces. With rising costs, this amount per man per annum went up to $2,000, that is from $1,400 to $2,000, in April, 1953, and now is again increased to $2,360, but it is still below the amount charged the British Columbia municipalities for the services of the British Columbia provincial police in the early part of 1950.
Supply-Justice
Now, as to the increase in rate planned for 1957, that is this increase in rate to these larger municipalities, this is based simply upon the conclusion that municipalities getting mounted police services should pay a higher proportion of the average operating costs. The percentage of federal work carried out by our men in any small town is relatively small. That is to say, we have contracts with provinces; we have contracts with rural areas and small towns, and we have contracts with larger cities. In the division of the cost per man that we have arrived at in all these cases, we try to reflect the proper share as between federal work on the one hand and provincial or municipal work on the other that the individual member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police does in the work he carries out day by day. We say that the percentage of federal work carried out by our men in a small town is relatively small. But the larger the town the more the men are tied up with routine town duties such as town traffic control, street patrol and desk duty-this was the point raised by the hon. member for New Westminster. In small towns and rural areas, federal, provincial and municipal work can be bulked together in an economic way, but this does not apply to the same extent in larger towns and cities where regular shift duty is called for. Furthermore, the larger the municipal detachment the more supervisors of the N.C.O. rank are needed, and thus the average rate of pay for the detachment becomes noticeably higher. Again, the commissioned officer in command in the area must give more time to larger detachments than to smaller ones. Having these facts in mind, it was decided to offer small towns a rate based upon 50 per cent of operating costs per man, while large towns would be asked to pay 75 per cent of this cost, the new rates to apply in 1957. I think I could quote the odd newspaper editorial-and perhaps I should. I refer particularly to one in the Vancouver Herald of June 2 which bears the heading "Still a Bargain" and says this:
Ottawa is moving to raise from $2,000 a year to $2,300 a year the charge for each R.C.M.P. constable engaged in provincial or municipal police duties.
Even at $2,300 it is a bargain. That is only 40 per cent of what the service costs. The federal government pays the other 60 per cent.
Who in British Columbia would want to go back to the old days when we had a separate provincial police force and communities outside of the big cities maintained their own local constables?
The R.C.M.P. in the B.C. areas which it polices has given the highest standard of service free from political or local influences.
It will always stand to the credit of Gordon Wismer that while he was attorney-general, he brought in the R.C.M.P. to replace the provincial and local forces.

Supply-Justice

With what was said as to the standard of service given, we are all in agreement, and we also agree that we are fortunate in being able to have this service from the R.C.M.P. But I think there is a fallacy in the argument which finds its application in a different percentage to be paid as between municipalities of different sizes.
After all, what are these municipalities contracting for? They are all contracting for the same thing, and that is local policing. I do not see how it can be described as other than a fallacious argument-and before I discuss it further, do I understand that the division point is 5,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

I was about to say that I do not see how it could be considered as other than a fallacious argument to say that a municipality of 4,900, which rates identically the same service in the matter of local policing, should pay less for it than a municipality of 5,100. I know that whenever a division has to be made it does become perhaps just a little absurd to take two examples, one of which is just above and the other just below the divisional point.
Nevertheless, while I recognize that weakness, it points up the fallaciousness, or perhaps I should say the unsound basis upon which the whole arrangement is placed. Because both these municipalities, even if there is a difference of 2,000 in population, are contracting for and receiving exactly the same service in the form of a local police service. Why should one municipality pay a different rate for it? I am unable to understand why that should be so. In both cases there are both federal and municipal responsibilities. The R.C.M.P. would have to carry out the federal responsibilities in any event; so all they are contracting for is a local police service, and I cannot see any logic in having it at two different rates.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I infer, and I hope correctly, that my hon. friend himself has admitted the weakness-perhaps weakness is the wrong word-in what he has said. It is really a platitude to say-
It was a reductio ad absurdum, showing the absurdity of the situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, that is right; but I suggest it shows only the absurdity of my hon. friend's example.
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is true that where one is trying to draw a line between one group and another, if it happens in a concrete case that it is very close to that line on either side, then the fact that the line comes between

the groups that are quite close to each other may perhaps set up an injustice. However, that arises from the fact that the line has to be drawn. And when a line always has to be drawn, that type of injustice sometimes is unavoidably encountered.
I can tell my hon. friend that the line drawn at 5,000, as in this instance, is, as I indicated earlier, that division above which would require over five men. And it is the cost of the men that really forms the basis for the manner in which the line is drawn. When you get above that line, then as I have already indicated you get into the matter of town traffic duty, more non-commissioned officers, and additional overhead of a civic police force in which you must face a number of costs on top of the men who are actually doing the police duties. You do not encounter these in the smaller towns and in the rural communities.
However, we do not pretend to be infallible by any means. If my hon. friend feels strongly that we are wrong, and if he feels he has good reasons he could submit to us, we would be glad to adopt his reasons if we find them better than ours, and apply some other division. But the division we have chosen is that made by those experienced in police work over long terms of years. And until my hon. friend builds up a more plausible case than he has thus far, I would prefer to rely upon their experience.

I am not so much concerned with the fact that the line is drawn at 5,000 as with the fact that a line is drawn at all. Because my argument is that both municipalities, namely the one above and the one below the line, contract for and receive exactly the same service. And the fact that in a larger municipality you will have to have more men, not only to do the actual policing but, because of the larger number required, to administer and supervise, is all compensated for by the fact that the municipality will have to pay for that greater number of men.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Would my hon. friend not admit that a police force the duty of which is to do both federal and municipal or provincial work-in this instance we will say it is municipal-in a rural area will find that the policemen will do a far larger percentage of federal work than they will in the larger towns or cities? That is the basis for the division.
In these rural areas we say, "We absorb 60 per cent because, as near as we can figure it, we are using that man's time 60 per cent of the time." I think we do not use him that much, and perhaps we are giving

the benefit of the doubt very distinctly to the municipality. But we say when we get into a different type of municipality, one more urbanized, that our man cannot spend as much of his time doing federal work. Therefore we have to raise the cost to the municipality, which is reflected by the fact that the police officer is spending more of his time doing municipal work.
In all these cases we have to convince the municipalities that they are getting a square deal. I believe we have succeeded in doing so. They are under no obligation to renew, and if they do not wish to carry on they are free to make their own arrangements.
Has the minister had any representations on this subject from the provincial as well as municipal governments in British Columbia, or were the representations confined to municipalities?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.

Where there is a detachment already established in a town, taking care of the surrounding district, and the town wishes to enter into a contract for its policing service, would it be possible to do so by using the presently established detachment, despite the fact they are short of manpower?

But there is a detachment already there, and the town officials seem to feel it would be quite possible for them to undertake policing the town while they are doing the surrounding districts. I am wondering whether it might be possible for a contract to be arranged under those circumstances?

The answer to my hon.
friend's question is yes, Mr. Chairman; it is having that effect. What one must remember in that connection is this. I mentioned this before. At one o'clock the committee took recess.

Mr. Chairman, there is one phase of law enforcement which comes under the R.C.M.P. which I should like to discuss at this time. I intend to comment upon the enforcement of the law in Canada in connection with narcotics, ask the Minister of Justice to comment upon this, and make a recommendation before I am through. Under our precedents and procedure an hon. member of this house is not permitted to make derogatory statements about the other place, its members or its committees, but I do not know of anything which would prevent an hon. member of this house making an honest comment upon an official report from the other place.
We have all received from the distribution office copies of the proceedings of the Senate committee on narcotics. I realize fully that the question of treatment could, not be discussed under this item as that would be handled by the Minister of National Health and Welfare; but law enforcement does come under the Minister of Justice and the R.C.M.P. and it is that phase of the matter on which I desire to speak.
I do not know of any report that has ever come to my attention over many years as stupid and contradictory as the report contained in No. 15 of the proceedings of the Senate committee on narcotics. This contains the findings and the recommendations and I assure you that I am going to deal only with the matter of law enforcement. I deprecate very much that in this report a vicious, unjust and unwarranted attack should have been made upon the narcotics division of the police force of the city of Vancouver. This report dealing only with law enforcement is most contradictory in nature.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
On a point of order, I rise most reluctantly because I do not want to interfere with the arguments of the hon. member for Vancouver East. I rise simply to question whether it is proper for us in the House of Commons to discuss a report from the other place in the manner in which my

hon. friend is now doing. I have no personal views at all; it is a question of order for the chairman to decide as to whether it is proper to do that; but I would question that it is.

Mr. Chairman, I thought I made it clear when I began that I knew the rules and procedure and I would not say anything derogatory to the other place, its members or committees. My only reference is to a printed report. After you have said that this is a printed report officially in our hands, I should like to continue. Criticism has been made against the law enforcement in the province of British Columbia. Sir, this is why I rise. Basically, although they are not mentioned, it is actually a major criticism of the R.C.M.P. and their narcotics division. I do not agree with that indirect criticism. I maintain that the statements in this report No. 15 on the law enforcement are most contradictory. I should like to draw to the attention of the Minister of Justice the admission of the committee that the R.C.M.P. have certain responsibilities. I refer to report No. 15 under date of Monday, June 20, of the proceedings of the special committee of the Senate. On page 657 it is stated very definitely:
The Canadian legislation dealing with narcotic drugs is contained in the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act . . .
This statement was made, and I shall quote from page 657:
By administrative arrangement the R.C.M.P. are responsible for the enforcement on the criminal side of the legislation.
I agree with that statement. They go even further. If you turn to page 660 of the same report No. 15 you find this:
The R.C.M.P. maintains drug squads at those centres where attention is indicated, reinforced as necessary by men from general duty and other specialist details. Most major municipal police forces maintain special narcotic drug squads which work closely with the R.C.M.P. The R.C.M.P. concentrates particularly on the investigation of traffickers.
I believe it is obvious from those two quotations that there was the recognition that in Canada the R.C.M.P. are responsible for the administration of the law as it deals with narcotics. We also have in the quotation I have given from page 660 the admission that any special drug squads of city or municipal police are ancillary to the R.C.M.P. That is why I say I deprecate the vicious and unwarranted attack on the Vancouver police and, in particular, on their narcotics squad.

I say to you, Mr. Chairman, and to you, the Minister of Justice, that I have had a great deal to do with them over a period of years, and I think they are doing an excellent job.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wonder if my hon. friend will just tie up his logic a little. Why does he interpret criticism of the Vancouver narcotics squad as an attack on the Royal Canadian Mounted Police?

If what is outlined on pages 657 and 660 of the Senate report is correct, the enforcement of law is the responsibility of the R.C.M.P. as regards narcotics. I think they are doing a good job. I am trying to help you. Do not interrupt.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have no objection in the world, Mr. Chairman, to my hon. friend helping me, but surely he will not object if I try to understand how he is helping me. Let us see whether I understand my hon. friend rightly. He says that, because of certain statements in this report to the effect that certain responsibilities attach to the R.C.M.P. and because the Vancouver narcotics squad has been criticized in that report, and because he interprets the first statement about the responsibilities of the mounted police to include those things for which the Vancouver police were criticized, therefore in the result this report is a criticism of the R.C.M.P.
I had understood that this report in fact was quite laudatory of the R.C.M.P. I would say that where the people who prepared the report are specifically laudatory it would be rather straining the meaning of the report to argue, by the process of logic my hon. friend is applying, that they were indirectly criticized.

I still have not come to page 664 of the report. On page 664 there is the following:
The committee could not help but be disturbed by this large concentration of drug addicts and the apparent freedom with which they are able to congregate in the heart of the city of Vancouver. These people are known to engage in crime, including prostitution, and are without gainful employment of any kind. The committee is not able to understand why the provisions of the Criminal Code dealing with vagrancy, prostitution tMr. Winch.]
and living off the avails of prostitution cannot be more effectively invoked to uproot and break up this concentration.
The committee, in emphasizing this aspect of the situation, points out that the enforcement of the Criminal Code in the city of Vancouver is not a responsibility of the R.C.M.P., but is wholly a responsibility of the city police authorities.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is the point.

But let us look at the next paragraph. It reads:
The R.C.M.P. are concerned with the enforcement of the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act and in this connection concentrate essentially on the apprehension and conviction of drug traffickers.
Sir, you cannot put all these quotations together and make them coincide. That is my point. You just cannot do it. I come now to what may be a primary point but is not the important one. The commissioner of the R.C.M.P. gave evidence before the committee and we find in this report that he says that from their investigations they know, and they must know, that out of the over 2,000 criminal addicts almost 1,700 were criminals before they were addicts. So it is a most important question for the R.C.M.P.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Would my hon. friend permit a question at that point?
Well, do not take it off my 40 minutes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If they were criminals before they were addicts, would they not as criminals fall within the responsibilities of the Vancouver municipal police?
I am sorry but I could not hear the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If the 1,700, to whom my hon. friend refers as being drug addicts, were criminals before they became drug addicts, would they not, both as drug addicts and as criminals, fall within the responsibilities of the Vancouver municipal police?
As addicts and traffickers they come under the R.C.M.P.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Oh, no.

You can speak when I am through, and I would be glad to answer any questions. Perhaps I am not putting this as clearly as I should. According to my understanding of the law of Canada and these sections of the Senate report, enforcement of the law regarding narcotics is primarily the responsibility of the R.C.M.P. An attack has been made on what I call an ancillary section of the enforcement of the law, the narcotics squad of the city of Vancouver. I think the committee was trying to take the

government off the hook so far as enforcement is concerned, and I think it did a disservice to Canada in doing so.
From my own personal knowledge of British Columbia, and British Columbia is being castigated in this report, the narcotics squad of the Vancouver city police and the narcotics squad of the R.C.M.P. have done and are doing an excellent job in trying to control the situation in the province of British Columbia. That is very definitely my opinion. It is proven by the number of arrests. It is proven by the number of men and women in jail and in the penitentiary in British Columbia and in the women's penitentiary at Kingston. I am not boasting about the fact. I am just saying that the narcotics squads of the Vancouver city police and the R.C.M.P. must be doing a job because half the women in the penitentiary are there for narcotics violations and come from the province of British Columbia.
Irrespective of whose responsibility it is and whether the Vancouver city police have fallen down-and I do not think they have- the major point is this. It was admitted by the Minister of National Health and Welfare when he appeared before the committee, and has been admitted by the committee itself, that we have a serious narcotics problem in the Dominion of Canada. Under the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act the major responsibility, I repeat, is on the R.C.M.P. We would not have a narcotics problem in Canada if drugs were not illegally coming into the country. I think that is axiomatic. Under the act the responsibility of preventing such drugs coming into Canada is that of the R.C.M.P. There is a statement at page 658 of the report of the committee which I was going to term challenging, but I really do not know what to call it. It is a pearl, a jewel.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What page is that?

Page 658. It reads:
The evidence indicates that, while Canada maintains excellent domestic control of licit narcotic drugs, international controls have not completely stopped the illicit flow of drugs into Canada.
Isn't that a honey? In Canada we have excellent domestic control of these drugs, which is fine, but international controls have not completely stopped the illicit flow of drugs into Canada. I gather what is meant by that is that it has not been found possible yet to stop the growing in certain countries of whatever it is from which the opiates and the heroin are derived. That is very regrettable, but it has nothing whatsoever to do with the fact that these drugs are entering Canada illegally. Our control is here and it is our responsibility, even if they are grown in
Supply-Justice
other countries, to stop them coming into Canada. If we stopped them we would not have any drug problem in Canada.
I am not criticizing the Minister of Justice or the R.C.M.P. one iota. With all our thousands of miles of coast line and international border there is a problem. There is no question about that, and I repeat that I think all police forces, the R.C.M.P. in particular, are doing the best they possibly can to prevent the illegal entry of drugs into Canada. I do not think there is any question about that at all. However, in view of this report and the publicity there has been in editorials and otherwise, we now have an admission of the terrific narcotics problem we are facing in Canada. Because I believe, and rightfully so, that the major responsibility is on the R.C.M.P. who, in my estimation, have done a good job, I think we are doing a disservice to Canada when the Minister of Justice does not ask for a great deal more money so as to concentrate on the building up of R.C.M.P. narcotics squads irl order to do an even better job of stopping the illegal flow of opiates into our country.
With the question of treatment I cannot deal at the moment. It is the matter of enforcement with which I am concerned. Mr. Chairman, you are not going to solve the problem of drug addiction by arresting people on a charge of vagrancy as suggested in this report No. 15. I am convinced in my own mind that the police forces of Canada- and I will mention that of the city of Vancouver-and the R.C.M.P. know who are the higher-ups in the drug traffic in Canada. But there is a big difference between knowing certain things and being able to obtain the evidence in order to lay a charge. I appreciate that fact. I think the Minister of Justice knows that I am correct when I say that the R.C.M.P. and the police of Vancouver have a great deal of information but that there is a big difference between knowing something and being able to prove it.
All the evidence is conclusive that the narcotics situation in Canada is costing Canada many millions of dollars a year in money and that is costing a great deal in terms of suffering in lives. In view of the situation existing, and in view of the cost in lives and in dollars, I should like to suggest through you, Mr. Chairman, to the Minister of Justice that an investment that will pay great dividends will be action at this session greatly to increase the amount of money available to the R.C.M.P. so that they may greatly extend their narcotics squads throughout Canada in order to do two things: First, to put a greater pressure on the stoppage of the illegal entry into this

Supply-Justice
country of narcotics; and second, to enable the R.C.M.P. to get the evidence they require in order to catch the higher-ups and to catch the traffickers. I maintain that the expenditure	of a	few extra	thousand dollars	oreven	a few hundred	thousand dollars	to
reach this objective is in the interests of the Canadian economy and of the Canadian people.
I should like the minister-and I am going to speak now in conclusion-to recognize that what	I say	is not by	way of criticism.	Ibelieve that	the police	of Canada are doing
a good job, but I believe that they could do a better job if they had more money and more men. I maintain that the investment of more money and more men in an effort to solve the narcotics problem is one of the finest investments that Canada could make at this time.

Mr. Chairman, I think all hon. members of the House of Commons, or at least most of them, have had the opportunity of reading some if not all of the reports from the other place with regard to the narcotic drug traffic in Canada. While I had not exactly reached the same conclusions as those reached by the hon. member for Vancouver East, I should certainly like to put myself on record as thoroughly endorsing the recommendation of the hon. member for Vancouver East.
If they have shown nothing else, I think the reports of the committee of the other place have shown us the seriousness of the drug traffic in Canada, particularly in western Canada. If the minister could do anything to increase the enforcement of the law in relation to the prevention of illicit drugs coming into Canada, I think this action would be of great benefit to this country.
There is only one further remark in this regard that I should like to make and it is this. I think the minister might take under consideration appropriate ways and means of stiffening the penalties against people who sell drugs, particularly those who sell drugs to young people. To my mind, those who sell drugs to young people commit a crime that is worse than murder. I should like the minister to take that matter into consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak on one branch of law enforcement in Canada which I think might well be handled by the R.C.M.P. but which is not being handled by them at the present time. Around these parliament buildings here I understand we have a branch of the R.C.M.P. law enforcement officers and I understand

that law enforcement around the buildings of parliament here is being looked after by them.
A year ago I asked the minister, on one occasion, who is responsible for the maintenance of law and order before committees of the two houses of parliament where people take an oath to testify and to tell the truth and nothing but the truth, and where it is thought that people may have perjured themselves. At the time the minister's reply was that this was the responsibility of the attorney general of the province of Ontario. When he was further questioned-I believe it was by the Leader of the Opposition-he followed through and said that anyone who had knowledge that perjury had been committed would logically have the responsibility of supplying that information and seeing to it that adequate action was taken. Then, in the fall of last year, we observed that action was taken in the case of two individuals, that a conviction was obtained, that the conviction was appealed and that the appeal was sustained on the ground that the houses of parliament were not courts of justice.
I am coming to the point in a moment. I feel that the R.C.M.P. has a role to play here under the direction of the Minister of Justice. I feel that the maintenance of the dignity of the parliament of Canada is the direct responsibility of the minister, with the aid of the law enforcement officers at his command. It may well be that there are constitutional difficulties that must be overcome. However, I am sure it is not beyond his ability to propose remedies that will take care of the situation. I know that this year the minister, upon further questioning, has stated that the new Criminal Code-which became effective last April 1, I believe-now looks after that situation. However, I should like to point out to the minister that a great loophole is still left. I agree with him that chapter 51 declares the parliament of Canada to be the equivalent of courts of justice in this respect. However, it still leaves unanswered or at least not answered satisfactorily the question as to who is responsible for seeing that action is taken. I think we agree that it is too much to expect the attorney general's department in the province of Ontario to concern itself overly much with all the evidence being submitted to the various committees of both houses of parliament. I think it is also too much to ask individuals, many of whom may have no personal interest in the matter whatsoever, to assume the initiative and see that action is taken.
When we know full well that there are rings of operators in existence who should be looked into, then I think the least the

minister can do would be to ask for a committee, or to ask for an investigation on the part of the R.C.M.P., so that these rings in what I shall call houses of ill repute can be investigated, and that these men who very brazenly, openly and unashamedly will supply false witness under oath, thereby degrading and making a mockery of the oath as it is administered to them before the houses of parliament, will be looked after.
