speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I raise this point of order, that when we move on from the item for the mounted police to discuss some other part of the esf'mates for the Department of Justice, undouotedly we will reach a point where the observations of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam would be in order. If we must deal with this matter then we might as well clean it up while we are at it, because it is a very simple matter, a very simple matter indeed.
The point, and I think they teach it now in high schools is, as to the distinction between provincial and federal responsibilities. Where the British North America Act says that the administration of justice and the enforcement of law is the responsibility of the provinces,

Supply-Justice
it means just that. Even in those cases where we proceed under the Combines Investigation Act to prosecute in any province, under a federal statute, I secure the permission of the provincial attorney general before launching a prosecution.
If there were any disagreement among informed persons about this matter I might see some point in the present instance in my hon. friend's statement. But in the course of his own remarks he cited a case in which a prosecution was launched that went to the Ontario court of apoeal. And it was launched by whom? Was it by the mounted police? Certainly not; it was launched under the authority of the attorney general of Ontario. And in an endeavour to deal with perjury before a committee of parliament the attorney general of Ontario or his representatives in this prosecution recognized his constitutional responsibility. What my hon. friend from Burnaby-Coquitlam wants to do, either because he misreads or does not understand the British North America Act, is to have the whole nation change the procedure which both provincial and federal authorities are agreed is the proper one.
The case which went to the Ontario court of appeal, under a prosecution launched under the authority of the attorney general for Ontario, turned, when it got to that court of appeal, upon the wording of the section of the code under which the prosecutor chose to lay the charge. The Ontario court of appeal held, as a technical point, that within the meaning of that section of the Criminal Code, as it then was, a committee of parliament was not a court. But their judgment was based upon the meaning of that section, and did not hold that parliament was not a court in the larger sense referred to, for example, by the hon. member for Prince Albert. But when you lay a charge under a section of the Criminal Code, then if there is any doubt as to interpretation that doubt is resolved in favour of the accused; for criminal statutes are interpreted strictly as against the crown. In Canada we try not to convict the accused unless we can prove the case completely.
Upon that technicality, and upon the wording of that section of the Criminal Code, as it then was, there was a finding by the court of appeal to the effect that the conviction- and it was a conviction-should not stand.
I explained in the house before, that when the Criminal Code was being consolidated we recast that section in a form that would obviate that kind of result in a similar prosecution hereafter. Therefore, if the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam knows of any case of perjury that is taking place before

a committee of parliament, it is a very simple matter for him to walk down the street to the crown prosecutor and tell him what it is all about so the prosecutor can investigate it in the same way he does any other crime, lay the information and carry on from there. If he lays the information properly under the relevant section of the new code, the result of the case should be different from that which went to the Ontario court of appeal. The fact that this case did go to the court of appeal in itself is proof that what I have said in this house on previous occasions and what I am saying now is quite right, namely that the responsibility for the administration of justice-the responsibility for that prosecution-rests with the provincial authorities. And it is not only a responsibility, it is a provincial right. I may inform the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam that when we met together in dominion-provincial conferences upon constitutional amendments there was not any provincial right under our constitution which is regarded with more jealous care by the provinces than their power over the administration of justice and the enforcement of law.
In this conference to decide as to whether there was any way in which we could amend the constitution in Canada, without having to go to the British parliament, this particular clause, clause 14 of section 92, was regarded by both of the large provinces of Ontario and Quebec as a part of the constitution which should not be changed except with the unanimous consent of every province. What the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, in his lack of knowledge of this subject matter, is suggesting is that we should go heedlessly ahead in an invasion upon this area which the provinces regard with such great care.

It is not desirable to get this point raised by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam into too technical a field, but surely the minister will admit that there is room for the suggestion that it would not be an unwarranted invasion of provincial jurisdiction to say, when the offence is committed within the confines of the parliament buildings, as these offences are, where they are peculiarly related, as they are, to proceedings before parliamentary committees, that he, as Attorney General of Canada, has a responsibility. If he as Attorney General of Canada were to see that these proceedings were commenced, to say that that would be an invasion of provincial rights is, I think, far-fetched and fantastic. It is a position that no provincial attorney general would ever take if the proceedings arose out of things that took place in these parliament buildings.

Incidentally, I might point out that the parties concerned in those proceedings come from another province. Why should the attorney general of Ontario be saddled with the responsibility of bringing criminal prosecutions against people from another province? It is true the crime took place here. It seems to me it is being far too technical with respect to this matter of invasion of provincial rights to say that we cannot lift a finger in this matter because it would be resented by the attorney general of Ontario. I should think it would be welcomed by the attorney general of Ontario and by those of us who wish to see that perjury is not committed here.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do suggest to the hon. member for Kamloops that perjury is no less perjury and is no less a crime, and its prosecution falls no less under subsection 14 of section 92 of the British North America Act, if it is committed in the parliament buildings, any more than if it were committed in some store on Sparks street or in Queen's Park; it is still perjury in every one of these cases. The enforcement of the law and the administration of justice still remain the responsibility of the attorney general of the province. It is still recognized by him as his responsibility The very case that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam cited was the case in which the attorney general acted. It is not merely a question as to what police force is acting here; it is a question as to who is going to have the carriage of the prosecution, who is going to decide what kind of charge is to be laid, or whether a charge is going to be laid at all.
There is only one way, in my judgment, that the provincial rights under any of these British North America Act headings can be respected, and that is by respecting them. That means that the federal authorities should leave them alone, as a field to be exercised by the provincial authorities. If the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam could come into the house and say, this is a great abuse. The provincial authorities will not do anything about these cases, they will not prosecute. Then we might give thought to what should be done. But the provincial authorities have prosecuted; and because they lost a case in the court of appeal upon the then wording of a section of the old Criminal Code, his argument, if I understand it rightly, is that the Attorney General of Canada should step into the picture. I may point out to him that if I, as Minister of Justice of Canada, had undertaken the responsibility for the prosecution which it is not my constitutional responsibility to do; if I had laid this charge under the same section the result would have
Supply-Justice
been just the same, because it was not the identity of the prosecutor, it was the legal point that was involved that produced the result that my hon. friend deprecates.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Rising in response to my hon. friend's suggestion, I first of all would like to thank him for the complimentary references which he made to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police narcotics squad.
I have worked with them over the years and I believe they are trying to do a good job.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:

as minister in charge of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, I have found they have done a first-class job in all of their undertakings. It would be quite exceptional if in their narcotics work they did not do their usual good job. I do not profess, even as the minister in charge of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, to be an expert in narcotics prevention; therefore I am reluctantly unable to express any opinion with regard to the quality of the work the Vancouver police are doing. With regard to the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver East that we should have more money, may I say that I do not suppose there is a department in any government that did not think it should have more money. My hon. friend says we should have more money wherewith to increase our narcotics squad, to the end that we might stamp out the importation and wholesale trafficking which is our peculiar responsibility. In general I suppose one might think that if X good men can do a good job, X plus Y number of men could do a better job; but I do not think it is quite as simple as that. This narcotics problem has received a great deal of attention from the Department of Justice, which is mainly responsible for one part of it. The Department of National Health and Welfare is also involved in the problem. I -believe there are views extant to the effect that there are perhaps better ways of stamping out narcotics than to merely add to the number of the narcotics squad, whether it is a municipal or federal force. For example, I believe the views entertained by people who are well informed in this field are that perhaps if the addicts who constitute the market, the only market in which it is profitable for these traffickers to deal, were all institutionalized there might cease to be a market.
That is fine; I am going to discuss that under health and welfare.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That might be a more potent method of stamping out the traffic than by

adding to the number of the narcotics squad either in Vancouver or in Canada.
There are now 4,200 addicts in Canada who are getting all they need daily, and it must come in illegally.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Quite true.

I am going to discuss this again under health and welfare, but all I am talking about at the moment is enforcement. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As I said a few moments ago, it can be argued that at the present moment the traffickers and smugglers are importing enough to take care of 4,200 addicts, therefore with a larger staff in the narcotics squad to stop importation that would have a salutary effect. I know that is one of the suggested solutions. But in addition to other solutions, there is the one I have just referred to. If these addicts were all institutionalized and were supplied their drugs by other than illegal means and the market thus was dried up completely, there would be no purpose in anyone importing drugs illegally.
The hon. member for Vancouver East knows very well that this whole matter is under investigation at the present time, as to which of these and other alternative methods is the best. In the meantime I appreciate his solicitude with regard to our end of it, and the support he has given for an increase in our appropriation.

Mr. Chairman, before the item carries I should like to have a little chat with the minister about communists in this country. Surely nearly everybody must be worrying today about communism in this country, yet we seem to be getting nowhere fast in dealing with it. The communist movement seems to be growing, not only in size but in intricacy and effectiveness and, shall I say, audacity. It seems to me that it is getting to the point where it rather defies the authorities to do anything about it. I should like very much to have the minister bring us up to date in respect of this matter.
The minister will remember that last year I suggested it might be wise to set up a royal commission to investigate the whole matter, because I felt that there were many aspects of communism of which the majority of people in Canada had not the slightest concept. Most people have the idea that communists become communists because they think communism is a better way of managing

the country and creates a better economy than the capitalist system we are using. They think that is about all there is to it. As a matter of fact that is just the least of our worries about the thing.
Communism as I have come to see it is the result of a terrible conspiracy of evil men who are setting out definitely to conquer the world and bring it under their own domination. That fact should be made manifest by a public investigation such as a royal commission, and that is why I suggested it last year. At that time the minister thought such a royal commission probably would be more injurious than beneficial, and he so expressed himself. I wonder if he would care to make a comment now after another year of experience in the matter. I am sure it must be troubling him terribly. The minister indicated this, in fact, when he was discussing the matter of the police. He indicated that there were so many security problems to take care of which constituted a sort of first charge on the energies of the mounted police and their members that it was becoming increasingly difficult to spare mounted police for other work.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I agree with that. We have freedom of speech in Canada, including the houses of parliament, and I think the hon. member for Lethbridge has the right to exercise his freedom of speech. The objection I would make to his remarks on the present occasion is that they are not relevant. They have to do with the C.B.C. and they are not relevant to the R.C.M.P. That is the ground upon which I base my objection. If he would raise these points when they are relevant it might be to better purpose.

I do not wish to offend at all. One of the big difficulties in connection with the radio committee and most of the other committees is this. All that goes on in them goes into their Hansard and people never hear about it. How many people read the Hansard of committees? How many people get to know what goes on in them?
You should. If you want to know what is going on in the radio committee, why do you not read their proceedings?
The hon. member can just wait until I am done, until after I have said what I have to say.
Go ahead.
If there is anything foolish in what I have to say, the hon. member can find fault with it.
Go ahead.

If it is foolish it will reflect on me.
The reason I am connecting it up with the R.C.M.P. is that, as the minister must realize, the problem faced by the R.C.M.P. in dealing with communism today is much worse than it was five years ago, and it is much worse than it was ten years ago. In other words the problem is increasing. No wonder that is the situation when by so many means we are indoctrinating our people with communism. I am objecting to what the C.B.C. is doing because it is indoctrinating people by the hundreds of thousands through speeches by men like Matthew Halton.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

Is he advocating that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police should control the schools, the universities, the radio and all the rest? In other words, is he advocating the establishment of a police state in Canada?

The hon. member asks if he can ask a question. Then he rises and asks a stupid question, when he knows perfectly well I do not advocate that. He asks that question because he knows that a certain press will report what he has to say and will not report what I have to say.
Oh, no.

There is that press which is ignorant enough to quote anything the C.C.F. have to say because they are interested in communism and socialism. I think I can refer to a good many reports, now that the hon. gentleman has asked me that question. He knows that in what I have said here I have not even hinted at such a thing. What I am suggesting is that the minister, as a responsible minister of the crown and a member of the cabinet, ought to be able, somehow or another, to exercise some influence over the C.B.C. If the C.B.C. is doing work which is making it hard for him to do his job, certainly he ought to be able
Supply-Justice
to exercise some influence on C.B.C. programs. That is all I say. That is simple enough. I think even the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar can see the logic of that, without my advocating a police state or any other monstrosity.
I am now going to pass on from the C.B.C. except just to read a little quotation which indicates that I am not the only one in Canada who has recognized this situation. I am quoting a summary report from the Winnipeg Tribune of Thursday, May 26, 1955. It is headed "I.O.D.E. Ask C.B.C. to Broadcast Fuller Reports on Communism". It reads in part as follows:
Members of the national chapter I.O.D.E., at the final session of the 55th annual meeting, Wednesday afternoon, in the Royal Alexandra hotel, passed two resolutions aimed at counteracting subversive propaganda and the threat of communism. One asked that the I.O.D.E. urge the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to make more extensive use of its facilities to bring to the attention of Canadians the menace of communism;-
I do not think it ever does that. All the programs I have heard indicate what a lovely thing communism is. The article continues: -that programs be provided in which members of ethnic groups recently arrived in Canada may take part, in order that they may relate unhappy experiences suffered in countries behind the iron curtain, thus helping to counteract subversive propaganda and the threat of communism.
You never hear of anything like that; oh, no, not at all. Although I do not think I will do so, I could refer to instances because I have a monitor who keeps very careful tab on the C.B.C. and reports to me most interesting things.

like having to interrupt the hon. member, but I feel it is my duty to the committee to do so. The hon. member has just said that he has a monitor who keeps him advised with respect to the C.B.C. We are discussing whether or not certain money shall be voted for the administration and other expenses of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I think I have said most of what I desired to say. It must be obvious that if a person were to hire a doctor to treat a case and then were to allow the patient to do half a dozen things that aggravated the malady twice as fast as the doctor could heal it, he would be exceedingly foolish to go on paying a high fee to the doctor. That is what it amounts to. I say that unless something is done by this government to prevent the incessant barrage of communism and the indoctrination of communistic ideals that is coming in over the radio waves of Canada, then this country is doomed to go communist in spite of everything we can possibly do. We might not call it communism, but people will go communist. It will manifest itself as communism in some form or other that one would not expect.
Then there are a number of other things I would like to mention. I would point out that this government, before the eyes of all people who really stop to think, stands in a rather questionable light. In 1946-and this still has a bearing on the R.C.M.P.-Igor Gouzenko brought to the government, very much against the government's will, certain revelations respecting communism in Canada. A royal commission was set up to examine those revelations. But just about the time the commission got started, somebody stopped it and left unexplored a great many of the leads they already had. They closed the whole thing up, almost with a bang.
Any ordinary person would ask, what caused that? What happened? What caused the government to close up that investigation? There must have been something. I am not going into any detail, though I have plenty more to say. I think I have said enough up to the present time. I am just warning; and it is my duty to warn, out of the knowledge that has come to my hand. If I fail to do that then I fail to discharge my responsibility, and that I do not intend to do.
Last year Igor Gouzenko came out of hiding. Evidently he was full of anxiety about what was going on, and he tried to warn this country. What happened? This government shut him up. Why was that? Who was it behind the government that shut him up? These are serious questions I am asking. I am not reflecting upon the integrity of the Liberal party, because there are in the Liberal party in the House of Commons some of the best men who ever sat in the house; the majority of them are like that. But that does not mean they cannot be the victims of very, very unhappy circumstances which it may be their united duty and
[The Deputy Chairman.]
responsibility-one which I am sure they will assume as soon as they realize it-to rectify, and without longer delay.
I am raising this question. If I were a member of the Liberal party, that is the first thing I would be asking everybody. Why did they shut off Igor Gouzenko? Why did they make it so hard for those investigators from the United States to gain access to Gouzenko? Why did they circumscribe those investigators in so many different ways?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not know what my hon. friend is leading up to when he suggests that the government shut off Mr. Gouzenko, because I think if he had been shut off by the government it is likely that I, as Minister of Justice in charge of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, probably would have known something about it. Certainly I have no knowledge whatsoever that he has been shut up in any way. Indeed, far from being shut up he wrote a book, a very excellent book, on his own initiative, a book which received the Governor General's prize for fiction and which proved to be one of the best sellers in this country and the United States. He appeared on a television program and radio programs in the United States and Canada. In the very case to which my hon. friend refers, when the investigating committee of the United States congress wished to ask him questions, we made arrangements for them to do so.
But I am sure my hon. friend, who is always fair in these matters, must realize that we, too, had a responsibility for the safety of Mr. Gouzenko. We had to make sure, in the arrangemnts that were made for his examination, that his security would not be jeopardized, and we were glad to do that. However, I must assure my hon. friend, as one man to another, that there is no foundation at all for the suggestion that we ever in any way shut Mr. Gouzenko up.
Except, Mr. Chairman, for the fact that we now hear no more about him.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No more about what?
No more about his revelations, about these spy rings that work in Canada and the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Well, the examination which took place on Canadian soil by the United States congressional committee was all reported by a Hansard reporter and they covered all that field in great detail. This was sent back with, if I remember correctly, the deletion of some 25 words from the whole

record. It was sent back to the United States government in that way. Is there any shutting up indicated in that?
Then with respect to what the hon. member has to say about spy rings, I would point out that that was so thoroughly investigated and resulted in such a large number of criminal prosecutions, most of which were successful, that even an important matter like that is subject only to a certain maximum amount of discussion, and when it gets beyond that point there is not much more to discuss.

We will leave the matter just at that, with my suggestion that it would be a most awkward situation if among those words that were deleted, there were names of some pretty high-ranking people in Canada. It would be most awkward, would it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I know my hon. friend wishes to be fair, but we like to clean up these things as we go along. As I recall it, the words deleted had reference to the nationals of a country other than Canada, and we did not think their names should be brought into a discussion which took place under our auspices. That was the reason we suggested that those words be left out. It had nothing at all to do with Canadians, and it had nothing to do with Americans, because we felt that if the United States committee wanted to take the responsibility for dragging any of their people into it that was their affair. But we did not think we in Canada should be the means of dragging into the discussion of an American congressional inquiry names of citizens other than Canadians.
And who might not be guilty.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, certainly; who might not be guilty. We did not think we should be in the position of libelling or slandering them, and the precautions we took to that end were, I think, proper ones. And I might say to my hon. friend that you cannot hide many secrets of that kind in 25 words.

I accept in good faith what the minister says. However, I would urge that he redouble his efforts in respect of communism in Canada. He knows that conditions are very serious, much more serious than the remarks of anyone, except myself, have indicated. And I can bring evidence, and plenty of it; I never have trouble in bringing evidence. I have one book right here which would be enough to make anyone in Canada have nightmares. I refer to this book "Pawns in the Game".

Some people get them.

Oh, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar comes along with his smart aleck remarks to get the press.

That will get the press; that very silly remark has been caught up, just as silly remarks have been made by other people just before their destruction. So I shall close what I have to say for the present. But I will be back again before we are finished with these matters.

Mr. Chairman, I have one or two questions I would like to ask the minister in connection with the R.C.M.P. My first question has to deal with young men who have joined the force. I do not rise to offer criticism, but to obtain information.
You take them into the force when they are 18 years of age. I think that is the age they have to be to join the force. You train them for a year or more. I think of my own experience in the army. It took longer than a year to be trained as an efficient soldier. I guess it takes longer to train to be an efficient constable. When they join they sign an agreement or give a pledge that they will not get married for seven years. Is that so?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, it is not so; it is five years.
What is the regulation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Five years, not seven.

Take a young man who joins when he is 18. He cannot get married until he is 23. Many people get married before they are 23. In the meantime you have trained that man from the time he was 18 until he is 21. He thinks differently at 21. He thinks he would be better off to get married. I understand he has to resign then because he has not carried out the agreement he signed. Is that so?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No. I think what we had better do is get the exact figure for my hon. friend. With regard to the policy itself, perhaps I should say this by way of explanation. As I am sure my hon. friend, with his knowledge of the rural parts of our own province, at least, would be the first to realize a great deal of the work of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police throughout Canada is in outlying parts of the country. We have had this rule because we feel we have to maintain a certain percentage of the force in a position where they can be moved about freely. When he enters the force the candidate knows perfectly well what these rules are. He knows he is entering into a contract whereby, in order that we may have a certain part of the force that can be moved around in quite out of the way places where it is quite difficult to find proper accommodation for a wife and family, we expect him in those first five years in the service to remain single. He knows that when he enters the force, and if he falls in love afterwards, well then he has to choose between carrying on with his contract and getting married. It does not take him by surprise. He comes into it with his eyes open from the beginning.

Mr. Chairman, I was out of the house and in my office for a few minutes. I understand that the hon. member for Lethbridge made some reference in his remarks to communists in my riding, especially in Uranium City.
Over 500 there.

I should like to make some remarks on that, Mr. Chairman. A communist ran in my riding in the last election, and naturally any communists there would vote for him. I do not like the idea being sent abroad that there are a lot of communists in the riding of Meadow Lake. It is a riding that occupies 40 per cent of the province of Saskatchewan. According to the official report

I hold in my hand, only 177 votes were cast for the communist candidate in the last election.
As regards the area of Uranium City, some remarks were made to the effect that the unions there are communistic, or something of that kind. I do not know whether that remark was made, but I should like to comment on it. I hold in my hand the statement for the 1953 election of the various polls in that area, covering any polls that were put in separate mines where the unions operate. At the Gunnar mine 66 votes were cast, and there was 1 communist vote. At the uranium mine of Nesbitt-LaBine there were 50 votes cast; there was 1 communist vote. At the Eldorado mine 179 votes were cast, and there were 3 communists. At the Rix mine, 38 votes were cast, and there were no communist votes. At the port of Bushell, where freight is unloaded and where some union men are employed in that work, 34 votes were cast and there were no communist votes. Therefore in the total for all the mines and the port of Bushell there were only 5 communist votes.
Then we get down to Uranium City. There were 226 votes cast, and a total of 7 communist votes. Therefore in the whole area of lake Athabasca there were in all 12 communist votes. I would take it that is the sum total of the number of communists in that area.
As I say, there are only 177 communists in the whole riding, according to the votes in the last election. The idea that the unions there are different from people in any other part of the country I reject entirely. I meet these boys from time to time when I go in there to discuss problems with them. I have met them individually and collectively. I do not think you will find that they are any different from any cross-section of workingmen in the country. They are hard-working fellows; they are good fellows, and I have yet to find one who is a communist.
As my hon. friend knows, I have no more love for communists than he has, but I hate anybody to be splashed with that paint if it is not justified. With these remarks, Mr. Chairman, I resume my seat.

I am sure the hon. member will desire to know that I read a quotation from the first article in the Reader's Digest of June, 1955, and that is all I said about his constituency. I would suggest to the hon. member that he write to the author of that article and tell him the facts. He probably

I received a letter in today's mail dated July 5, from the automotive retailers' association in Vancouver, signed by J. L. Kinneard, addressed to myself at the House of Commons. I should like to draw the minister's attention to this matter. It states:
As a member from British Columbia, you are aware of course of the charges that have been made against this association and a good many of our individual members by the combines commission.
You are no doubt also familiar with the brief that was presented to the Minister of Justice which did outline the position of the retailer in B.C.
In spite of the information contained in this brief, the department appears to be adamant in their determination to pursue this matter.
Our members, although they do most sincerely believe that they have done no wrong, are now called upon to defend themselves in a major action through the supreme court against charges which, in all fairness, should never have been levied. You can readily understand why this is a matter of very real concern to our members.
For any small businessman to face the almost impossible task of financing an adequate legal 
defence in the court, is in itself a problem and a worry, but added to this has been the humiliating treatment given to these businessmen at the conclusion of the preliminary hearing.
The enclosed bulletin has been sent to each of our 1,200 member firms along with a copy of a letter to Senator McKeen. It was thought they would be of interest to you.
There is more to this matter, Mr. Chairman. There are other bulletins. I am satisfied the minister did receive the brief that was mentioned in the letter. However, reference was made to some particular treatment in respect to these businessmen of which I am not so sure the minister knows.
At the time this investigation was first launched, some 30 businessmen in the retail gasoline business in British Columbia-that is, service stations-were charged with entering into a combine contrary to the act. The magistrate who was in charge of the preliminary hearing suggested, at the time they were notified to appear on the 12th of April before the supreme court, that no bail would be required, since the men are creditable businessmen and would be released on their own recognizance.
On April 12 these men presented themselves to the court. They were lined up in the regular fashion as a group while a formal announcement was made to each one of the group as to the charge. They thought they would merely have to sign a paper indicating who they were and that, as suggested, no bail would be required. Instead of that, they were ushered into one of the cell blocks and kept there for from one to five hours, depending on their particular turn, and removed from the cells three at a time. They were fingerprinted and were then permitted to sign and were sent on their way.
This, of course, was a humiliating experience. They were treated as criminals to begin with. Their only crime was doing something that is being done every day by the major business firms in this country. They are a group of small businessmen who have got together and -are charging a particular price for gasoline, in the same way Loblaw's stores or the Dominion stores in this city get together and sell butter at the same price on one day and may decide to sell pork and beans at the same price on the following day.
It is possibly true that we have ian act that indicates they are a combine because they are not associated in a limited firm under one head, and therefore have not the right to carry on this particular practice. Unfortunately this situation has arisen as the direct result of an act that was in effect at an earlier time. Prior to 1937 in the province of British Columbia conditions were quite

chaotic, as they were in other parts of this country. The Macdonald commission was set up at that time, which made certain definite recommendations to the provincial government of the day, who in turn passed those regulations on to a coal and petroleum control board. I am not satisfied in this instance that there is a need for a combines investigation act. I wish to establish that to begin with. There are certain phases of the act itself which might well bear some revision. I am thinking more particularly not about the case I mentioned earlier, but instances where we have small grocers who are in an awkward position when they cannot make agreements with each other or small businessmen who cannot make agreements to sell a product at a particular price. They have no protection under the act. They are guilty of having a combine once they decide to sell

a product at a certain retail price on a specific date and at a specific time.
We have business houses which make it a practice to establish prices in a particular way, and I am thinking at the present moment of such instances-not with any criticism-as the Gillette company of Canada which advertises ten razor blades for 50 cents and five for 25 cents. As a matter of fact I understand that it is not necessary for the people who sell these blades to adhere to these particular prices. However, the suggested retail prices are there. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am very much embarrassed about interrupting my hon. friend again on a point of order, but earlier this afternoon the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, who has to keep an engagement very shortly, asked me if it would not be possible for him to raise before he left a point he wished to raise under the vote for the combines branch. With the unanimous consent of hon. members, would the hon. member for New Westminster be willing to give the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar the floor for that purpose at the present time?

I may say to the minister that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar indicated that situation to me earlier today. At the time I began to speak he was not in the chamber and I had this problem to put forward, but I shall be only too happy to give way to him.

Thank you very much; I appreciate it. As a matter of fact I had just gone upstairs to sign some mail. The point I am raising is there has been some discussion in the city of Winnipeg regarding what appear to be certain collusive understandings among the sugar refiners as to the price of sugar, particularly in Manitoba and the city of Winnipeg. It looks as though there is a working arrangement among the sugar producers of Canada. Price lists were recently issued by the sugar companies making their sugar price changes effective on the same day, May 18, 1955. The times on this date

Supply-J ustice
when the changes were to go into effect did not vary by more than an hour or two.
I have the price lists here on my desk, but I am not going into them in detail. What happened on May 18 was the same pattern that was followed with respect to their price lists on May 3, 1955, March 31, 1955, and so on. As far as the price lists are concerned, if they are investigated by the combine authorities-and I hope they will be-I am sure they will find some very interesting material upon which they can work. The lists are issued a day or so apart, and the times the changes go into effect are almost the same. Of course it would be possible, if one company had produced a price list, for other companies to produce price lists shortly afterward, but these seem to have been issued simultaneously and without any prior information to the trade. It strongly suggests that there is some working arrangement, and I suggest to the minister that the combines investigation organization might look into sugar prices in Manitoba.
The price lists I have looked at strongly indicate that the Manitoba Sugar Company and the other companies shipping sugar into Manitoba have come to an agreement. Whether it is formal or tacit I do not know, but it certainly is mutually profitable to them. These are the facts as I have them, and I want to be quite quick about the matter because I realize our time is limited.
The Manitoba Sugar Company, producing at its Fort Garry plant, has an annual capacity of 40 million pounds of white granulated sugar. I take that information from the Financial Post report on industrials for 1954, the latest information I have. The Fort Garry plant does not produce enough sugar to meet Manitoba's requirements. Consequently Manitoba must import sugar from the east. The price of this sugar is the laid-down cost of sugar at Montreal plus freight. Because the price of the total supply of any commodity is dictated by the cost of the most expensive portion of the required supply, Manitoba consumers are compelled to pay for all of their sugar the laid-down cost at Montreal plus freight from Montreal to Manitoba. This places the Manitoba Sugar Company in the very advantageous position of charging a higher price for its share of the supply, approximately half of the Manitoba market, than sugar companies charge consumers elsewhere in Canada. In other words, for each pound of sugar the Manitoba Sugar Company produces and sells in the Manitoba market it receives a bonus equal to the cost of shipping from Montreal although, of course, it does not have that expense.

I am not going to give the details of its profits, which are very high indeed. On the 6 per cent cumulative preferred shares of the company the experience has been a profit of $20.76 per $100 share in 1951, $20.42 in 1952, $16.35 in 1953 and $14.91 in 1954; in other words, about 20 per cent. These profits, of course, are very high indeed. It appears quite evident from what I have been able to ascertain that the arrangement, whether it is formal or tacit, is profitable to all the companies because if the Manitoba Sugar Company produces one-half of the amount required in Manitoba, the other half is supplied by the eastern companies, and that gives them an opportunity to dispose of any surpluses they may have.
On the face of it this seems to be a case into which the investigating authority should inquire. I am going to leave the matter there because I have just had a note put on my desk that this is the private bills hour, and I do not want to intrude on the time of the house when it is allocated to other business.
However, while I have been very brief and have only given a very sketchy outline, I am going to say that from the price lists I have on my desk it appears that these companies issue their price lists on approximately the same day, almost at the same hour, and that their prices are the same all the way down except that the Manitoba price is a little higher because of the addition of the freight charge. The contention I am making is that this causes the people of Manitoba to pay a higher price for sugar than is warranted. In my opinion it also tends to restrict the production of sugar in Manitoba if it is deliberately kept at half the Manitoba supply in order to maintain profits. It is also in the interests of the importers of cane sugar in eastern Canada, and it does injury to the Canadian economy. I leave the matter there.

subtopic: DONALD JOHN MCGILLIVRAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I spoke on this bill last Tuesday my remarks at that time were based on the evidence I had heard in the House of Commons committee on divorce, and I must admit that while I did not hear all the

evidence I heard that portion which was given by the two paid investigators. Of course it was on that evidence that I based my remarks.
While there is no record of that evidence printed, possibly it is just as well. In one respect I suppose it is rather fortunate from the point of view of those who would have this divorce go through without too much trouble. I think possibly the fact that that evidence was not written down is rather fortunate from their point of view. But for those of us who are trying to show that this case does not warrant passage it is rather unfortunate that the House of Commons committee on divorce does not have recorded minutes of their meetings.
After reading and studying the report of the committee of the other place in connection with this particular bill there are a few other aspects about it, in addition to the ones I mentioned the other day, which have prompted me to rise and speak at this time. I do so in spite of the fact that those of us on this House of Commons committee are being quite pointedly criticized by the members of the committee of the other place who question our judgment, and question whether we are competent to question the decision they have made with regard to any case that comes before them.
Before saying anything further I should like to apologize to the house for one remark I made last Friday, when I said I did not realize that we had a side-show going on in this House of Commons. Once again may I say that I was completely amused at the part of the evidence which I heard. But since I have read the verbatim report of the evidence given in this particular case before the committee in the other place I must say that I have uncovered, to my own satisfaction, one or two other aspects which I think are of tremendous importance. It is of those aspects that I wish to direct the attention of this house this afternoon.
I said it was a side-show. But in the sideshows we do not see children being sacrificed. It is because of that aspect that I feel we should give the greatest consideration to this matter. After examining the evidence I cannot help believing that the husband in this case is conniving to place his wife in a somewhat compromising position whereby he would have grounds for divorce. I do not come to that conclusion because the wife has said in her evidence that the husband "propositioned" her as to whether she would be willing to give him a divorce. While she says that in her evidence, I am not so gullible as to believe that she is totally without blame.
Private Bills-Divorce
I am not here this afternoon to make a case for either the husband or the wife as such, but I am here to try to draw to the attention of this chamber the serious situation that can develop if a divorce is granted where children are involved. I am quite willing to give both of them the benefit of the doubt. They have made a bad deal. But regardless of whether or not they have made a bad deal, they have some responsibility to any children that may have resulted from that union. A divorce should not relieve them of that. I believe court proceedings do not and should not relieve any couple of their responsibility to children. It is up to us to see that they accept their responsibility. It is up to us to accept our responsibility to see that they accept their responsibility. That is the one basis on which I have raised this matter this afternoon. I want to see that we are fair and that the child in this case has some protection.
While it is not a nice thing to be confronted with a proposition of this kind, if we are to do it the justice we are asked to do it I believe we must be as fair as we possibly can. Regardless of what the husband thinks of the woman and regardless of what we may think of her-those of us who listened to the case; regardless of all those things- there is one fundamental fact that we must face up to and it is this. This woman is looking after the welfare of the child. We cannot deny that fact. This girl is 12 years of age. I contend that this girl is at an age at which she needs her mother. At possibly no other time in her life does she need a mother as she needs one at this critical age. Regardless of what we may think of the mother, she is better than no mother at all; and that is something.
Just how bad is she? We know that she is getting only $80 a month from her husband. She has two daughters by a former marriage, and they are contributing $10 a month each. One of those girls is married and has a family of her own, but she still thinks enough of her mother to contribute $10 a month, along with her unmarried sister who is 20 years of age. This woman of whom we hear so much has taken a companion for her daughter to this cottage at the lake for the summer. On an income of $100 a month, she is certainly not a very selfish woman when she will take a companion for her daughter. You cannot accuse her of that shortcoming. If she were selfish, she would not do that.
On the other hand, what responsibility does the father feel he should take for his daughter? Let us take a look at the other side of the picture. When he was confronted by the attorney defending the woman involved
589S

Private Bills-Divorce
he was asked if he had any other motive besides trying to find his wife in some compromising position whereby he could get a divorce. He was asked, was there any other motive. He answered, "Absolutely none". He said that was not the motive. He said he did not care anything about getting a divorce. He said that was not his motive for making this investigation. But what was his motive? As to that I should just like to read from the evidence. The question was:
Did you have any other interest in going there?
That was to make a preliminary investigation. His answer was that he was not interested in getting grounds for divorce. He said:
Why should I provide her with a summer camp?
He would throw this woman out, with the daughter; let us not forget that.
Why should I provide her with a summer camp?
But later in the evidence he admits that the woman, his wife, not only paid for a good share of the lot upon which the home was built, and not only paid for a good share of the lumber that went into that home, but that the title is registered in her name. I say that without question he connived to arrange for conditions to be such that he could sue for divorce.
There are a few very queer things about this case that require investigation. I could not help thinking that if I were going to enter an action for divorce there are two questions I would be pretty sure about. First of all, I would be sure of the date I was married, and I would also be sure about the date I obtained the separation from my wife. But how sure was this man? Just note these questions:
Q. When were you married?

But when he was confronted with his marriage certificate it was 1942, not 1941 at all. I am prepared to give him the benefit of the doubt. Perhaps it just seemed that long; I do not know. Then he did not know the year in which he obtained his separation. He was asked whether it was 1951 and answered that it could be, but that he thought it was either 1951 or 1952, approximately 1952.
Then when he was questioned by counsel as to when he first went to the cottage to spy on his wife, on July 4, he said that his suspicions before that date had never been aroused. Yet according to the evidence he said that he and his cousin made a tour of the property on July 4. Incidentally, he had not spoken a word to his wife since his separation from her in 1952, and this took place in 1954. He said he had never seen her or

spoken to her, and he was not suspicious of her until July 4. He was accompanied by his cousin, and he said:
We made a tour of the property out of sight behind and took up a position on an elevation. We could overlook the cottage without being seen.
Still he says he was never suspicious of his wife's actions until July 4. Well, he must certainly have been a very timid man, when he would sit for four hours spying on his wife's cottage if he did not have suspicions.
Then on August 13 he came there in the company of two detectives and the same cousin. And here is another strange thing. The cousin was with the husband when they sat for four hours watching the cottage. Under oath the husband swore that he built the cottage. Then, again under oath, when the cousin was being asked why he went along he said he went only as a guide to show the husband and the other two detectives where the house was. This was the man who built the cottage, but he had to take somebody else to show him where it was. Surely there is something suspicious about the whole situation.
Then let us take another look at the further information that was given. I am not going to say too much about the credibility of the two witnesses to whom I referred the other day, because I think that was dealt with rather fully. But from their evidence, together with that of the husband, it is obvious that the story does not stand up very well.
They say there was a party at the house on Friday, the 13th of the month, and that at two o'clock, after the party broke up, the four men-that is the husband, the cousin and the two detectives-went up to the cottage. But this cousin who went as a guide was smart enough not to go into the cottage and to have nothing more to do with it. About two o'clock they broke into the cottage. The husband said under oath that one of the detectives tried to force the door in with his shoulder. He could not do so, so they used a log. The other detective, giving evidence under oath, said it was not the detective but rather the husband who forced the door in. They both agreed they had to use a log to break the door in, but one of the detectives said they used a boulder to break it in.
So the whole evidence is confusing. I think the most confusing of all was when the husband swore that after the door had been broken in, the wife came out of the bedroom followed by the co-respondent. One of the investigators swore under oath that the woman was in the room when they broke in and later called to the co-respondent who

came out of the bedroom. The other fellow could not remember very much about it.
So we have such confusion in evidence that it is very hard to come to any clear decision as to who was telling the truth and who was not. All this evidence is completely denied by the other parties to the case, and so we are asked to make up our minds to what the facts are.
What about this evidence, which is denied so vehemently by the other parties to the case? What about the husband? What about the cousin? And then, what about the two investigators? I would say, after listening to the testimony given by these two gentlemen the other day before the House of Commons committee, that it is very hard for me to give them the benefit of any doubt whatsoever.
At this point may I draw to the attention of the house the evidence submitted before the committee of the other place in connection with the credibility of these witnesses, because I fail to see how anybody could have any faith in their evidence, it having been proven conclusively that the two detectives in question are absolutely untrustworthy. Here we have one of these investigators being asked before the committee of the other place:
Q. How long have you been a private detective?
A. About a year.
Q. Tell us the date.
A. Well, it was some time in the middle of August: I cannot tell you the date.
Q. The beginning of August, in 1954?
A. That is right.
Q. Did you have a licence as a private investigator in the province of Ontario?
A. No sir.
At the time the evidence in the case to which I have referred was given this investigator did not even have a licence to operate in Ontario. The investigator was asked this question:	'Were you charged before the
Ontario courts with fabricating evidence with intent to mislead a court of justice?" Again the answer was yes. So we have a witness giving evidence and admitting that in 1954 he had been convicted before a court of justice because he had fabricated evidence with intent to mislead a court of justice. Here is the remarkable part of all of this evidence. The chairman of the committee on divorce of the other place said:	"We
are not very much interested in that".
I do not see how that affects us. That is a matter between him and the province, or the crown. We have nothing to do with that.
Possibly that ruling was right, but it does not in any way take away the fact that here were men who had been convicted of fabricating evidence, giving the same kind of evidence before the same kind of committee, 50433-373
Private Bills-Divorce
and we are asked to listen to them and give them the benefit of the doubt in so far as their action of the past in fabricating evidence is concerned.
I feel we must give this case a great deal more thought than we have done. First of all, let us remember this. Here we have two people. I am not interested in them at all. They made a bad deal. But let us not forget that a 12-year-old girl is involved in this case. She is the victim through no fault of her own. What is to happen to her? Is she to be given any protection? Is she to be cast out into the world at an age when she should be under her mother's care? That is of the greatest importance.
If we have to deal with these cases it is our responsibility to consider them very carefully, to give the best we can in the way of a verdict for all parties concerned. Certainly in this case we should see to it that our decision is made in such a manner that we shall not jeopardize the future of this 12-year-old girl. The mother and the father made a bad deal, and now they are trying to get out from under their responsibility toward their daughter.

Mr. Speaker,
I am a member of the private bills committee that heard this case. When it was brought before us in the committee I voted against the bill. I do want to say a word or two as to why I voted against it, because I did not have an opportunity at that time, not that I could not have taken the opportunity but it was getting late. It was midnight, and I did not want to hold up the committee that day. But I could not bring myself to believe that the evidence submitted by those who were giving evidence on behalf of Mrs. McGillivray could possibly be discredited.
I listened very carefully. I am not a lawyer. I am not accustomed to having to sit in a courtroom and hear arguments, and I do not know that I would care to portray myself as an expert on the actual way in which evidence is submitted. But I do believe I have an ordinary amount of common sense. I have been in the position throughout life of having to deal with people and with human problems, and perhaps I look at evidence in a slightly different way from what a lawyer might. I look at the way in which it is presented. I try to watch the expression on the faces of those who are presenting the evidence. I try to determine whether or not those who are giving the evidence and testifying in the cases are telling the truth.
I could not help believing and concluding that Mrs. McGillivray and those who were testifying on her behalf were submitting to

Private Bills-Divorce
the committee that which they believed was the truth. On that basis as well as on the evidence, as far as that goes-because as far as I could see the evidence was just as strong on behalf of Mrs. McGillivray, the respondent, as it was on behalf of Mr. McGillivray, the petitioner-I voted against the bill.
I do want to say this in respect to the two investigators who appeared before the committee. I quite realize that sometimes investigators have to be tough. Their work is such that if they are not tough when they start off, after some years they often end up by getting tough. I realize that. But what I was going to say was this. I do not suppose there is very much we can do about it when investigators come before us who have been charged with fabricating evidence and their case is appealed and thrown out on a technicality which has nothing to do with the actual evidence. When that happens I cannot help feeling that their testimony is no longer reliable. I am saying I do not suppose we as a committee can do very much about it. I wish we could. I wish the private bills committee could have more power than it has when it arrives at a conclusion as to whether or not to pass one of these bills.
I know there are legal technicalities that have to be overcome, because we are dealing with matters that in many of the other provinces come under provincial jurisdiction. I believe that either the committee of the other place or ourselves should have a certain right to fix alimony. We should have something to say about the care of the children afterwards. I repeat, there are certain legal technicalities that stand in the way of that. I believe we should have some such powers, because very often there is a tendency, particularly among laymen to judging evidence and reaching a conclusion by taking all these other factors apart from the measure of guilt, to turn down a case not necessarily because we do not believe the case has been proved but because there are other factors in it which would be serious if we passed the bill. I think we should have the power to deal with some of these things.
I realize that we can do nothing about the fact that these investigators may have been charged previously with fabricating evidence, but I believe the attorneys who take these cases and are responsible for placing them in the hands of the investigating agencies should be told, if it is in our power to do so, that if they are going to employ investigators they had better come before us with clean hands or we will turn down their evidence.
I think if we went right to the seat of this trouble and spoke to these attorneys in that 
way and in no uncertain terms, it might help clean up this fabrication of evidence, if it is being fabricated. There is a strong suspicion held by some of us, and it has been held for many years, that it is being fabricated.
I want to put this on the record as my personal feeling in the matter. I have no sympathy with those who stand up in court or before a committee of this house or of the other place and take this oath, "I swear to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth, so help me God" and then barefacedly lie. I have nothing but the utmost contempt for such people, and as far as I am concerned they are not welcome before the committee.

I should like to express my concern about the apparent growing tendency to extend the grounds for divorce in this country. Divorce, by its very nature, is a social evil which should be fought with all the means at our command. It strikes at the family itself, basic element of our society. Take away the mother from her children and you destroy the family. The countries where, so far, divorce has been most prevalent are now facing the acute problem of an ever-increasing number of children without parents and, therefore, without protection. The communists themselves have found it necessary to repeal certain of their divorce laws since, after ten years of such legislation, they were faced with the responsibility for thousands of abandoned children.
In considering possible extensions of the grounds for divorce in this country, let us take heed of the victims of the separation of the parents. Let us think of those poor waifs doomed to become the castaways of life. It is unfortunate that more concern is felt about the plight of divorced parents than about the fate of their children. If we make it increasingly easier to get a divorce, too many married people will no longer think of establishing their home on a solid and permanent foundation. There will be a growing tendency to deprive marriage of children, whose presence in these conditions becomes embarrassing. Are we then to be surprised by the statement that divorce has become a social plague?
It has been said in this house, in the course of a debate on this subject, that if a couple cannot remain on good terms, they had better separate. A very appropriate reply was given to this sophism, which I should like to summarize in the following words: "Surely, it is better not to marry at all, if marriage can only lead to separation." Under a theory which favours the spread of divorce, the time will come when marriage will have lost all

that makes it a permanent institution and when more and more people will look for fancied incompatibilities in their partners in order to justify the perverse designs of a sinful separation.
The trouble with this moot question is that marriage, essentially a sacred institution, has been distorted and diverted from its real purpose ever since people are being led into it without reflection and without preparation.
It would be rash to believe that, by making it easier to sever the bonds of matrimony, society will be better protected. The function of any parliament conscious of its responsibilities cannot consist in aiding and abetting the establishment of a system fraught with such serious consequences and entailing such nefarious results.
Today, we often hear it said that there is need for more and more social security. Are we forgetting to what extent social security is weakened by divorce? We expect the state to be more and more generous towards the family; yet, on the other hand, through measures of this kind and in the name of freedom and civilization, we are weakening the family, the very basis of all social security.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I should like to quote remarks which are quite pertinent to this matter. Those remarks are from Msgr. Fulton Sheen, a religious speaker of international repute. I quote:
The family is the barometer of the nation. America is worth no more than its average family . . . if the ordinary husband or wife does not respect the oath of faithfulness made on their wedding day, America will not insist on respect for the Atlantic charter or the four freedoms. If people deliberately prevent the fruits of love from germinating, then the nation will adopt as its economic policy to plough under its cotton fields, to throw coffee into the sea and to interfere with nature for the sake of ensuring an economic price.
If a man and wife live each for himself and not for each other, if they are blind to the fact that their individual happiness depends on its being mutual, we shall then have a country where capital and labour will quarrel among themselves as husband and wife, both making social life fruitless and economic peace impossible. If husband or wife should let outside attractions estrange him from his spouse, we shall then become a nation where foreign philosophies will permeate, as communism is now sweeping that basic loyalty which used to be called patriotism. If husband and wife live just as if God did not exist, then America will have bureaucrats who will ask that atheism be set up as a dogma throughout the land who will repudiate the Declaration of Independence and who will deny that all our rights and freedoms come from God. Every country has the government it deserves. As goes the home, so goes the nation.

Hear hear!

Mr. Speaker, I am sorry I could not follow the hon. member for Kent, N.B. (Mr. Michaud), as my education was neglected in high school. However, I shall look forward with a good deal of interest to reading the translation of his comments.
On Wednesday of this week a question of privilege was raised in the Senate by the hon. senator who is the Conservative leader in that place, and I quote from page 767 of the Senate Hansard as follows:
Yesterday I sat in the gallery of another place during a debate, and I was very much hurt by the attitude shown by certain hon. gentlemen there with regard to a few divorce bills passed by this house. I do not know the details of the evidence adduced in connection with the particular divorce bills that were under discussion.	__
I should like to say, Mr. Speaker, that I have a very high regard for His Honour Senator Haig. He is a distinguished Canadian with a splendid record covering many years. I had no intention of hurting him or his other colleagues in the Senate. However, in Canada we have a House of Commons and a Senate. Just as the Senate reviews legislation passed by the Commons and approves or disapproves of that legislation, so we in turn have the responsibility to examine carefully all legislation originating in the other chamber and brought before us.
However, I should like to endorse what His Honour Senator Haig said on that occasion:
I have some suggestions to make with regard to our divorce proceedings, not in criticism of the operations of the present divorce committee at all, but on the over-all problem of divorce procedure in this house, particularly on the question of how we should handle divorces, in view of the rising criticism in another place.
Later on in the last paragraph he stated:
I thank the house for permission to make these few remarks. I hope that between now and next January, or whenever parliament shall reassemble, honourable senators will consider this whole matter and come here prepared to offer suggestions as to how this very, very vexed question can best be handled.
I should like to endorse what Senator Haig has suggested, and to add that the House of Commons might have a committee of members of all parties to join with Their Honours the senators and see if we cannot be relieved of this responsibility, which Senator Haig points out is a very difficult one.
I might mention that in Votes and Proceedings of the 1st of July there is a report of our miscellaneous private bills committee, of which the hon. member forParkdale (Mr. Hunter) is the chairman. While I do not agree with the hon. member for Parkdale on many issues, he is a very competent and very fair chairman who gets the business done with everyone

Private Bills-Divorce
feeling happy. When Bill No. 490 was considered the recommendation by our committee was that it "agreed to report the preamble thereof not proven on the grounds that the committee is not satisfied that the petitioner is worthy of having his petition granted."
I see no reason why Their Honours the members of the Senate should take exception to the fact that a responsible committee of this chamber should be unable to agree with their decision. My roommate, the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort, pointed out the fundamental question that we should consider in connection with this particular divorce. As he intimated, one could not say that the two sides who came here were perfect, that either of them had a perfect record or that one was all black and one was all white. In all these divorce cases there are always some problems that are not too easy to solve, but I think we should take into account that there is a 12-year-old child who at the moment is getting some assistance due to the fact that the father is committed to paying $80 a month in support of the mother plus $50 a month house rent, a total of $130.
That does not appear quite a fair distribution of the father's income, which seemed to be in the range of $4,000 a year. Certainly this 12-year-old girl should not be placed in the position where the father has no further responsibility in connection with her upkeep and education.
I think the members of this house will have to decide this case on the basis of the evidence which was presented to the Senate committee and our committee by good solid citizens, as described by the hon. member for Macleod. The people who appeared on behalf of Mrs. McGillivray appeared to be a good cross-section of Canadian society who felt that this woman deserved favourable consideration. Their stories compared very well when told in the Senate committee and when told here. On the other hand, we are asked to grant a divorce purely on the evidence presented to the Senate and to our committee by two gentlemen, Pichette and Santerre. Mr. Santerre was questioned before the Senate committee as follows:
Q. Did you have a licence as a private investigator in the province of Ontario?
A. No, sir.
Q. Then at the time of this episode of August 14 or 15-
A. Morning of the 15th.
Q. -you were not a licensed investigator in the province of Ontario; is that correct?
A. No, sir.
Q. Mr. Santerre, were you charged before the Ontario courts with fabricating evidence in divorce matters and with operating as a private investigator without a licence?
A. Charged with fabricating, yes, sir.

Q. Were you found guilty and the sentence
appealed?
A. Yes, sir.
Q. And were you liberated on bail?
Here is an interjection which, I think, would not have been made by the hon. member for Parkdale as chairman of our committee. Senator Ross, the chairman, said:
We are not interested very much in that, are we?
The solicitor for Mrs. McGillivray said:
Well, if that is the ruling, sir.

I don't see how that affects us. That is a matter between him and the province, or the crown. We have nothing to do with that.
I am very sorry that, whilst I have known Senator Ross for many years and I know he is a learned lawyer and a fine citizen, I cannot agree with him when he ruled that this type of questioning was not of interest to those who were going to decide whether or not these particular gentlemen were reliable witnesses. Let me remind the house that these two gentlemen were tried in Ottawa last November by His Worship Magistrate Strike. The charge was that the appellants-
-with intent to mislead a court of justice, did unlawfully attempt to fabricate evidence by means other than perjury or subornation of perjury.
It was argued before our committee that this charge was laid last November and these two men secured the evidence last August. Whilst their behaviour was contemptible in November, we had to decide whether or not the evidence they discovered last August was or was not to be accepted by our committee. I should like to give members of the House of Commons some idea about these gentlemen. Again I do not ask you to take my impression of them, though one of them certainly misled me when I asked about his status. I asked whether or not he had a licence to practise in Ontario, and he admitted he had not. I did not see how he could operate in this province without a licence, and he explained that as long as they were hired by the Montreal office they could work in Ontario or any place else in Canada, as a matter of fact. But later he admitted under cross-examination that he had paid a $200 fine for acting as an investigator in Ontario without a licence.
How do these two men operate? These are the facts as presented to Magistrate Strike and on which he convicted them. They never appealed on the basis of these facts. The facts, as set out in the judgment of the appeal court, are as follows:
The appellants, desiring to obtain evidence for the purpose of enabling a married woman to secure a divorce, planned to trap the husband into a false position from which adultery might be inferred or found if evidence was later given in some proceeding for divorce. This plan was to have

a woman go to a room in an hotel, register under an assumed name and give the room the appearance of the bed having been occupied. She was not required to do anything more. The husband was to be lured by a pretext to the room and, when there, could be found by the two appellants, who would then be in a position to give evidence as to his being found there with the woman. In carrying out this plan, the appellants arranged with woman "A" to obtain the hotel room and perform her part of the plot, which she did. In the meantime, the appellants arranged with woman "B" to call the husband, under an assumed name, which was the name which woman "A" was to use at the hotel, and invite him to come to the room. This was done by woman "B", but the husband was suspicious. Woman "B" claimed to be a friend of the husband's sister, and the husband took the precaution of calling his sister as to the friend whose name he had been given over the telephone. Instead of going to the hotel room as invited the husband went to the police, with the result that the plan at that stage miscarried and it was the police who went to the hotel room, instead of the two appellants who were endeavouring to mislead someone.
Last November Messrs. Pichette and San-terre were tried on this charge. They did not deny it and were found guilty. When the case went to the appeal court of Ontario it was heard by Mr. Justice Pickup, Mr. Justice Roach and Mr. Justice MacKay. The judgment continues:
The first ground of appeal is that the crown failed to prove the intent necessary to constitute the crime charged. It is argued that it was necessary, under the charge as made, to prove an intent to mislead a court of justice, and that the intent proved in this case was not an intent to mislead a court of justice but, at most, an intent to mislead the divorce committee of the Senate, and parliament which might act upon a recommendation of the divorce committee.
In view of that reference I cannot understand how Senator Ross was able to say that they were not very much interested in this sort of problem. I continue:
The residence of the husband is shown by the evidence to be in the province of Quebec, and from that it may be inferred (there being no evidence to the contrary) that the domicile of the husband was in Quebec and that any intent to mislead must have been an intent to mislead the Senate committee of parliament and not a court of justice. This ground of appeal, therefore, turns upon whether or not the Senate committee and parliament are a "court of justice" within the meaning of section 177. In my opinion, they are not. The expression "court of justice", in the sense in which it is used in this statute, in my opinion, should be given the meaning attributed to the word "court" in Murray's English dictionary, vol. II, p. 1091, col. 1, under item 11, from which I quote the following:
"An assembly of judges or other persons legally appointed and acting as a tribunal to hear and determine any cause, civil, ecclesiastical, military or naval."
Underneath this definition, the editors write:
"Justice was in early times administered in assemblies held by the sovereign personally . . . then by judges who followed the king as officers of his court; hence the title the King's Courts. In this sense more fully defined as court of law, law-courts, court of justice, of judicature."
