speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
May I just give some information that I promised the hon member for Burnaby-Coquitlam this afternoon. He asked this question: "Can the minister state why this item for $20,000 for grants to recognized prisoners' aid societies-that is in vote 160- should appear in this item and also in item 170?
The answer is that this item for $20,000 under vote 160 is the amount which is paid to prisoners' aid societies for their work in assisting and counselling prisoners who have been released on ticket of leave after they are outside of prison, whereas the item for $40,000 under vote 170 is compensation for the same kind of work extended to prisoners while they are in prison; that is in visiting them, maintaining liaison with their relatives, finding work for them while they are still in prison and the like.
May I ask the hon. member a question?
Certainly.

Did the hon. member say that Loblaws, Dominion stores and some of the other big retail stores are meeting together to agree upon prices, or that Loblaws, within its own firm, sets its own prices only?

I would say more directly that Loblaws within its own firm, and Dominion stores within its own firm, and Canada Safeway within its own firm, through its central directors, dictate what shall be the price within a certain community on a particular day. Possibly there is a certain amount of discussion. There is an indirect combine, I might say, in this respect. If Loblaws have a particular price on a commodity, even in this town, Dominion stores send their pricing man around to their various stores on a particular day, possibly once or twice a week or possibly every day, in order to discover whether their prices are in line, as they call it. If they are not in line, they bring their price down to the other mark.
That may be to the advantage of the public as a whole. I am not going to discuss or try to determine whether or not it is, because you find that if a staple item such as pork and beans drops from 15 cents to 14 cents a can, in all likelihood on that same day tomatoes went from 15 to 16 cents a can in order to retain the differentiation. But you have there in effect an indirect combine, if I may call it that. There is no set argument, but it arises by reason of the fact that one can go about and establish for himself what the price is in the other store, then bring his price into line. I see no difference in effect between that and the large store or several large stores getting together and saying, "We are going to charge 15 cents for a particular item and raise the other one to 16 cents" and then sending trouble shooters or price finders around in order to find out what others are charging for staple items and so vary their prices accordingly. The public is gaining nothing. It is being fooled into thinking that because the price of a particular

item is lower one day in one store, it is not going to go down to that same level in another store at another time.
But what about the manufacturer who takes a pride in his product-and I am getting away from groceries now-who not only offers the product but also offers quality and service? I am thinking, for instance, of General Electric tea kettles, where the manufacturer guarantees that if that tea kettle becomes broken in its normal use, let us say within a period of one year, he will replace it with a new one. A certain individual retailer may decide that he wants to make that item into a loss leader, and he uses it for that purpose.
I do not see that there is a case for the person who is going to sell this item as a loss leader, because he is not doing it with the help of the manufacturer but because of the fact that other similar articles are being maintained at respectable prices in other stores and the manufacturer is reaping a benefit from the sale. There may be more sales of that particular item on that particular day for even a short period of time, but in the over-all picture the price establishes itself and levels off.
In order to meet such competition another individual may purchase tea kettles of an inferior quality, bearing no brand label, and palm those off on the public. We often hear the phrase "Let the buyer beware;" no doubt the minister has heard it. The article being offered carries no guarantee, as does the article offered by the manufacturer who is trying to peg the price of his product. The result is that the purchasing public is the loser, because when it makes a purchase no guarantee is given. The manufacturer of the better article wishes to keep the price at what he considers a reasonable level. He knows full well that if he is going to offer that kettle with a guarantee, his merchants must get that price for it if they are to remain in business.
Earlier today the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar drew to the minister's attention what he described as a combine in the price of sugar. I would say most definitely that from every appearance there would seem to be a combine, and I would strongly urge the minister to examine into the matter.
The minister may ask why it is that on the one hand I seem to want an investigation into combines while on the other I oppose them. Perhaps in that connection I might draw these facts to the minister's attention. Where you have a maximum fine of only $10,000 against some of these giants of industry-

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think we should keep the record straight as we go along. There is no maximum fine now. It is unlimited.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend is thinking of the act as it was formerly, not the act as it is now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member will realize that in the prosecution of cases a long time is required in the investigational stage, with the result that there is an appreciable time lag. The courts are bound to impose the rate of fine set out in the law at the time the offence was committed. That is the main reason there have been so few heavy fines. In other words, it would not be fair to an individual or a corporation to impose upon them a fine that had not been enacted until after the offence was committed. It would be harsh upon an individual or corporation if it were made to pay a fine greater than that which attached to the offence at the time it was committed.

I realize the truth of what the minister says. Probably we will have greater fines from now on. I would say that a fine of $10,000 to a giant industry with unlimited credit is the equivalent of the fine of a bag of peanuts to a small operator. There we see evidence of inequality in the act. I have no doubt that if justice is to be done it must depend upon the administration of the act itself.
To make the act workable we should offer to small merchants or to other individuals in a community the same right to fix prices that is offered to the larger organizations, whether those organizations are in the form of giant supermarkets, such as we see today, where within their own organizations they can maintain certain price schedules, or whether it is found in other form. My point is that the same privilege should be given to the small group in a community which must compete against such opposition. If the ten Loblaws stores in the city of Ottawa -I do not know whether that is the correct number-and the same number of Dominion stores decide they are going to sell pork and beans at 15 cents a can, then it is only fair and just that the small merchants should be permitted to get together as a group and decide upon the price they want to charge. They should have the privilege of charging the same price if they so wish.

Supply-Justice
In connection with the sugar combine, to which the hon. member referred, it would seem that there is no factor of competition. For that, if for no other reason, it should be investigated very closely. Most certainly if a combine is found to exist, through price maintenance, then it should be held responsible for its actions. My thought is that under British justice we should have equal rights for all. I do not believe the Combines Investigation Act applies equally to the giant merchants-Loblaws, Dominion, Safeway or whatever they may be-and the smaller merchants. These large marketing organizations can establish their own prices and, in effect, constitute a combine within themselves.
Earlier I brought to the attention of the minister a letter from an individual in Vancouver having to do with charges laid against a group of garage men. My purpose in bringing the matter before the committee is to criticize the treatment these men received when they were taken to court to answer the charge. I explained to the minister the sequence of events, and I shall not repeat it. However, he can understand that it is a serious matter for a group of businessmen, respectable citizens who have been in the community a long time, who in effect committed no criminal offence. They were not guilty of any crime such as forgery, robbery, an offence under the narcotics laws, or any major misdemeanour of that kind. But these men most assuredly were humiliated and degraded before the eyes of the public in Vancouver by having to spend from one to five hours in the police cells, among hardened criminals. Then they were subjected to fingerprinting, and all this after they had been told that they would be permitted to go on their own recognizance. This was a stigma on their integrity and honesty.

Mr. Chairman, the minister, I suggest, should give some explanation of the manner in which these men were treated in Vancouver. After all, they are responsible citizens engaged in the service station business, and apparently they had been told by the magistrate that they would be released on their own recognizance. I am not blaming the magistrate, because Magistrate Scott is extremely capable and fair, and I do not believe he was involved in any way in what happened.
I would like to know whether the Department of Justice appointed a special prosecutor, because if one was appointed I imagine the fault could be laid at his door. Apparently when these men were committed for trial by a higher court, instead of being let out on their own recognizance in the ordinary way

they were locked in the police cells, some for as long as five hours. That sort of thing should not go on in a case of this kind. These men are only being picked out from dozens of others. They have done nothing different from dozens of other service station operators, and why they should be locked up in the jail in that way is very hard to understand. I believe the committee is entitled to an explanation from the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra was entirely correct in saying there should be an explanation, and the only reason why I did not start to give one was that he got to his feet quicker than I did.
May I say first of all that so far as the Department of Justice and the combines investigation branch of the department are concerned, we deprecate very much indeed what took place on this particular occasion. My hon. friends will appreciate the fact that it is an instance where, as I said earlier on these estimates today, we with the permission of the attorney general of British Columbia, are prosecuting for an offence which is peculiarly under a federal statute. This is a pretty good demonstration of why the administration of justice and the enforcement of the law should be conducted at the provincial level; for I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that it is very difficult indeed to conduct a prosecution some 4,000 miles away.
Three thousand.
Less than 3,000.
Don't put us farther out than we are.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The only course that is open to us is that which the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra mentioned just a moment ago, and that is to retain a prosecutor who represents us in the entire prosecution. On this occasion we retained one of the leaders of the Vancouver bar, a man whose name, when I mention it, will indicate his standing, namely Mr. A. E. Branca, Q.C.
I think in fairness to Mr. Branca, since we have had one side of the story, we should put on the record his side of the story which we got from him. Disturbed by these accounts and complaints which had come back to us, we got in touch with him and said, "For goodness sakes, what has happened? This is entirely contrary to our views about matters of this kind, and we would like to know how what took place here has come about."
I am now reading the account he gave us of what did take place, and I want hon.

members to take particular note of the precautions he took as far as it was within his power to avoid the very difficulties which arose. He says:
I was able to contact the responsible parties a couple of days ago and this is what happened. Prior to committal, in conference with Mr. Russell representing the person accused, and Magistrate Scott, nominal bail was agreed upon in order to facilitate the post-committal procedure.
For the benefit of the lay members of the committee, a committal takes place when a man is brought up before the magistrate and the crown produces enough evidence to establish a prima facie case against him and warrant his being put on trial. After he is committed for trial then normally, and certainly in a case of this kind, he is released on bail. In the present instance the special crown prosecutor, whom we had instructed before the committal, had conferred with counsel for the accused and with the magistrate and had arranged for nominal bail; that is just for a nominal amount for all these accused in order to facilitate what was going to happen if the committal took place. The letter continues:
Mr. Bill Edwards, the clerk of the court, had his staff working, he assures me, about two days in order to prepare the recognizances required in each case, in order to avoid any inconvenience or delay following committal.
The bail was arranged before hand; the recognizances were made out. In this case,
I understand, there are some 30-odd accused, so that the mere clerical work involved in making out committal orders, drawing up the bail bonds, and so forth, was quite considerable. In order to avoid any of these difficulties they worked two days in advance.
Committal took place in the courtroom, and the men were then taken to what is known as cell block No. 1 under the custody of Sergeant Mutch. It is true that in cell block No. 1 there were some other persons charged with some other offences, but the sergeant assures me that they were so placed as a matter of convenience in order that they might be handy.
"That they might be handy?"

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Handy for the purpose of
being fingerprinted with the least possible inconvenience to themselves. These were not defendants in this series of charges; they were other defendants.
The officers in charge even provided for a justice of the peace and a fingerprint man to be immediately outside of the cell in order that they might more promptly be released and discharged.
That is not the usual procedure but it was done in this particular case, for the convenience of the accused.
The usual procedure is to lodge them in a cell, advise the fingerprinting department, and they are then taken two floors up and fingerprinted, then held until the justice of the peace and the clerk's
Supply-Justice
department has prepared the documentation, and then brought down and released when the recognizance is perfected.
That is the normal procedure in committal on indictable offences.
This, as you will see, did not take place in this case, as the matter was prearranged as I have set forth in this letter. The sergeant assures me that the whole transaction took an hour or shortly more-
-and that is not surprising when you have 30-odd bail bonds to provide for, even if they are prepared beforehand.
In view of the fact that the copy of the letter that you enclosed is written in a critical sense-
We did get a very critical letter and we had sent that letter along to Mr. Branca and said, "What about it?"
-more particularly in so far as the police officers here are concerned, I took the liberty of discussing the matter with Mr. Russell and he tells me that his impression was that the whole procedure took somewhat longer, although he remained an hour or one and a quarter hours and waited with these men as some were released, and then left.
There is the explanation of what took place. I must say, in view of that, I do not really know what the special prosecutor could have done more than he did to expedite the release of these persons. The real difficulty in these cases is that we have a law upon the statute books, the Identification of Criminals Act, not passed with specific reference to combines offences but applying to all indictable offences, which provides that the police, where the accused is committed for an indictable offence, may take his fingerprints.
In the present instance apparently the municipal police, having developed a practice under this law and knowing that these were indictable offences and feeling that they would be taking on a pretty invidious responsibility if they undertook not to apply the law, did arrange for fingerprinting.
That has raised an issue which we are investigating at the present time. This is the first time we have encountered this sort of thing. We are considering in offences under an act of this sort what change should be made in the law or the practice to prevent the law from being applied in cases where, as here, there is no need to take measures for future identification. I can see, however, that if one were in the position of the police or the court officials they may have thought they had no alternative, although we think in fact they did. However, I really do not see how Mr. Branca could have done very much more than he did to expedite the whole proceeding.

I submit that it was highly improper for these men to be locked up in

Supply-Justice
order to be fingerprinted. I do not agree with the minister that the special prosecutor did all he could. He probably was not there at all when this happened, and it was his responsibility to see that these men were treated in the way in which they had every reason to believe they would be treated. Arrangements were made that they would get out on their own recognizance, and for the minister's prosecutor to try to get out of any responsibility by saying that this is the regular practice in the Vancouver police court is not a good excuse.
I think the minister should have this matter investigated by one of his own officials here in Ottawa, because this just about amounts to persecution. If you are going to have trouble of this kind with your special appointees this work might just as well be done by the minister's department. They should conduct these prosecutions so they will be conducted in the manner in which we all expect them to be.
What the minister has amounts only to an excuse or alibi from his specially appointed prosecutor, and I do not think that should be taken as full justification for what happened in this case. We know the way in which these prosecutors are appointed, and if this is the sort of treatment to be meted out to Canadians in prosecutions of this kind by these special prosecutors then I suggest to the minister that a different method should be adopted for the carrying out of these prosecutions.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not want to labour the point at all, but I think the account we have received makes it clear that counsel for the crown and counsel for the accused made these arrangements in good faith.
That does not say Mr. Branca was there when these men were locked up.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He was not there, but the arrangements were made beforehand.
He should have been there to see that the men were treated properly.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I suppose he might have been, but he attended with counsel for the prisoners beforehand and made these arrangements. I think in a case like this he did everything he was called upon to do, especially when the accused were represented by counsel.
I assure my hon. friend that we regret that anything like this should have happened, and so far as the department is concerned my hon. friend can be assured that we will take every step possible to avoid a result of this kind happening in the future.

Did the defence counsel indicate in the letter that it was agreeable to have them locked up in the cell even to go 
through the ordinary channels, or was it not understood beforehand that they would be let out on their own recognizance?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have laid before the committee all the facts upon which I could form any judgment. I think the members of the committee are just as capable as I am of forming a judgment. My impression is that the lawyers for the crown and for the accused arranged this thing beforehand, and they assumed that everything was going to be all right. To the extent that has been indicated here today it was not all right. I imagine that if a similar case arises on some other occasion the lawyers on both sides and we ourselves will make sure there will be no repetition of this kind.
I did not get what the minister said earlier in respect to a change. Is the minister investigating a change in the legislation to make sure this will not occur again?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
What I said was that the practice of fingerprinting arises under the Identification of Criminals Act, which has general application to all cases where a prisoner is charged with an indictable offence. The purposes of the Identification of Criminals Act are wholly praiseworthy. They are to obtain a series of fingerprints from all those prisoners who have been involved in indictable offences and whose future identification may be necessary. This fingerprinting system performs a great service to the police in apprehending offenders, particularly those who have records.
The offences here were indictable offences and I suppose the police said "Well, there is the act; what are we going to do about it? We will just follow the act". What we are now considering is whether the Identification of Criminals Act or the practice thereunder should be inapplicable to certain individuals or certain offences which now come under it.
Will the minister have an investigation of this occurrence made by someone in the department in Ottawa?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We could do that, but I do not know that there is very much to investigate. We have before us a clear account of exactly what happened. It is regrettable, but I certainly do not think there was any motive on the part of anyone concerned in the matter to produce these regrettable results. What benefit was there going to be for anyone to insist upon having these prints made?

I do not think there was any motive, but I think there was sheer carelessness on the part of counsel appointed by the minister's department. As a result these people were treated in a manner in which

they should not have been treated. I suggest that it is the responsibility of the minister's department to make a thorough investigation in order that cases of this kind may not happen again in Canada. Once there has been an investigation the minister can send out instructions when he appoints a person as prosecutor in a case of this kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is true, but I have already indicated that we are going to have a look at the Identification of Criminals Act in relation to matters of this kind. We are going to take all steps necessary to avoid a repetition of this situation.

I should like to have it clear in my mind whether the procedure followed in the case under discussion was different from the normal procedure followed when persons are committed for indictable offences.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The answer is no. The case put by the hon. member for New Westminster and the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra is that the indictable offences involved here were committed by people who in every other respect were most respectable and therefore they should have been handled on a different basis from people who had committed other kinds of indictable offences.
It is not only that; I think if the minister checks up he will find that people are not locked up in the case of indictable offences in order to be fingerprinted.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows from his own experience in acting for people who have been locked up that if 36 men were all committed at the same time in respect of what we ordinarily regard as indictable offences, such as armed robbery and so on, it is not likely that the police would allow them out of their custody while they were being admitted to bail. If they did, and as a result the prisoners walked out and caught a taxi and went away, the police would look rather silly.
But I do not think that because that would be so in the ordinary run of indictable offences, there was any similar reason that it would be in the present instance. The only real accusation that can be brought against the police is that they were unimaginative in applying the law and in acting according to its letter, in making arrangements for the control of the accused.

If one man were committed on an indictable offence and it had been arranged that he would be let out on his own recognizance, he would not be locked up in order to be fingerprinted.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He might not, but the point is that there were 36 here.
The minister could only justify such an action if the 36 were all trying to escape, and that would be ridiculous.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not trying to justify it at all. I am giving a factual statement as to what took place. I am not trying to justify it, nor am I trying to criticize those who had the responsibility. The police had 36 accused and the question was, while they were going through this procedure of signing all these papers, whether or not they would have them behind a locked door as a group. They chose to apply the same procedure to them as they apply in other cases of indictable offences under the Identification of Criminals Act.

That would be only true if there were 36 bank robbers there at one time. That is the parallel case. The minister says they acted in the same way as they would act if they had 36 bank robbers, and that is a thing that would never happen at all. If there were one or two men who were being committed on an indictable offence, they would not be locked up at all in order to be fingerprinted. It appears to me that through the negligence of the crown prosecutor, specially appointed by the minister's department, these 36 individuals were locked up. That is what we are complaining about. I hope nothing like this will happen again.

May I ask a question of the minister? If there were one or two men, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, mentioned, and they were not locked up, that would be because it would not be necessary to lock them up to ensure their presence. Therefore when there are 36 people they are locked up only to ensure their presence until the preliminary proceedings are completed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. My hon. friend has put a beautifully phrased leading question, the answer to which is yes, that certainly it is the only reason. My hon. friend is phrasing a question from his own experience as counsel in legal matters generally. I thought I had made it clear that when they are admitting 36 people to bail they are not really free until the bail bond is signed; so they keep them locked up in the meantime, as my hon. friend puts it, to ensure their physical presence.

From what the minister has said I gather that the 10 bread firms that were convicted some time ago would be locked up and treated in the same fashion, or the management of those firms.
