speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The bread companies were corporations which could not be locked up. These were personal accused. You cannot fingerprint a corporation, and you cannot lock it up.
What about some of the officers of big companies that have been charged? Have they been locked up too?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend should not get excited. If my hon. friend will go back through the records he will find that there have not been many occasions when officers of corporations have been prosecuted. In these particular cases most of the accused were individuals operating their own service stations, which were not incorporated at all. It was John Jones, or William Smith, or Peter White and so on. They were the ones who were parties to the alleged combine. It is because they were parties as individuals that this question arose in this particular case. As a rule when the offence has been committed by two or three corporations, there being no personal accused involved a question of this sort does not arise.
Can the minister give us one instance in which the officer of a big corporation was charged and locked up while they fingerprinted him?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I shall attempt to explain this again. If one man is concerned in this particular case and he appears before the magistrate, the crown's evidence is heard and the magistrate says, "Mr. Jones, I hereby commit you for trial". They have the bail bond read. He steps up in the courtroom and signs the bail bond. Having given the bail, he walks out. That might still be true with two or three. It could be done informally in the courtroom, as I have indicated. But if you have 36 there would be some of those 36 who would have to wait 45 or 50 minutes or an hour while the others were being taken care of.
Why lock them up?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Those who were responsible for them, that is the police officials and the officials of the court-not the crown prosecutor, nor the defending lawyer, who would not be present then-but the police used their own judgment as to whether they should do that. Apparently they played it safe and took no chances on not having the physical presence of all the accused when their turn came to be dealt with.

The minister's department
must take the responsibility for the manner in which this prosecution is being conducted. I think the blame comes right back here, and
[Nr. Hahn.]
the minister should have a thorough investigation of what happened in this case. It is obvious it was very unfair to these men.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

I notice that items 165 and 166 both deal with the Combines Investigation Act. We approved the principle of this act, involving a total expenditure of almost half a million dollars. I know the act has a deterrent value, and the investigations and the successful prosecutions that are lodged every once in a while also have a deterrent value in protecting the consumers of Canada.
However, after the bread combines were found guilty and made to pay a fine, I sat back and expected the price of bread to come down. The price of bread has not come down at any time since. Can the minister tell the house and the country whether there is any follow-up of the effect of successful prosecutions, or if there has ever been a case where a further prosecution has been launched? Does he know of any case where a successful prosecution has actually helped to reduce the price?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Prices of commodities at any given point of time are the result of a number of factors, only one of which is that measure of competition in the field which it is the purpose of this act to secure. When you are attempting to isolate the effect of a prosecution under this act and say that as a result of that prosecution the price has gone up or has come down, you have to be assured that all the other factors which bear upon that price have either remained constant or have not become less favourable or more favourable to a measurable extent than they previously were.
It is one of John Stuart Mill's rules of logic that if you are seeking to prove that a certain phenomenon is the result of a certain cause you have to make sure that all the other possible causes are accounted for before you can draw such a conclusion. Therefore it is really quite difficult to say positively that a reduced price which follows a successful prosecution is necessarily the result of that prosecution. What we do do after a conviction has been secured is to assure ourselves that there is no conduct upon the part of the accused which constitutes a further or repeated transgression in relation to that for which it has been found guilty.
I think that is about as far as we can go, because the Combines Investigation Act imposes upon the branch the responsibility of seeing to it that there are no combines which interfere with the free operation of competition, but it does not give us any

jurisdiction over the economy or over any of those economic factors which determine prices other than just that one.

What method is employed in the follow-up? I am very pleased to hear the minister say there is a follow-up. Is the follow-up a natural one as a matter of duty, or does the branch sit back and wait until somebody in the country launches a complaint that a combine again exists?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am sure my hon. friend will realize that when we have such a large variety of cases involving different concerns in different industries operating under quite different conditions, it is very difficult for me to generalize as to the steps that are taken. But in each of these instances we take those steps which we think are necessary in relation to the conviction and in relation to any of the facts that seem to be developing in that industry after the conviction.

Under the powers of the act can you only investigate if you think there is a monopoly or conspiracy? Is it possible under the powers of the act to investigate a discrepancy in prices of goods? I have in mind what is happening in the pharmaceutical industry. Health means a great deal to all our people, and when you have to pay for a prescription the cost is terrific.
I have evidence right here on my desk indicating that you can buy cortisone, one of the antibiotics, for a certain price under certain circumstances, but if you have to have a prescription for cortisone filled the price is 500 to 1,000 per cent higher. Under the legislation we are now discussing is it possible for the department to investigate such a matter and do anything about it, or can these people go ahead and charge what they like for these things that people need for their health?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In reply to my hon. friend's question, it is one thing to pass an act like the Combines Investigation Act which defines certain offences and in effect makes them crimes, and it is another thing to develop a technique of detection under the act. Where, as in the case my hon. friend speaks of, he finds that the price of some product seems to be extortionately high under certain circumstances, or where in another case the prices of a certain commodity that is being sold by a number of dealers all go up by a fairly substantial amount and by exactly the same amount at the same time, these are facts of which I am sure the Combines Investigation Act administration would take cognizance and investigate. But they would not necessarily prove an offence, because the offence is that
Supply-Justice
of different persons or corporations coming together to reach an agreement upon a fixed price.
If this high price about which my hon. friend speaks in the case of cortisone, which is much higher when it is prescribed than on some other occasion, is not due to an illegal agreement, then it is not the proper concern of our department. We are not a wartime prices and trade board that fixes prices. We are not an economic control body of any kind. We are the body which administers the act, and what we are concerned with are those prices which are the result of an agreement between people to fix prices and stifle competition, contrary to the terms of the statute under which we operate.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
B-Penitentiaries-
170. Administration of the office of the commissioner of penitentiaries, including $40,000 for grants to recognized prisoners' aid societies, as may be approved by the treasury board, $398,326.

Under this item last year the minister was kind enough to make a statement concerning the work of reform and rehabilitation that has been taking place in our Canadian prisons during recent years. I am sure all hon. members were quite impressed by the report he made on that occasion.
At the time I expressed my personal pleasure and also the opinion of the group with which I am associated in the house, but I also emphasized that in order to carry out successfully and thoroughly the new emphasis on reform and rehabilitation in our penal institutions it was necessary to give attention to more than the actual internal program that prevails in our institutions. It is becoming increasingly emphasized by those directly interested in the problem that actually you cannot go too far within the institution itself in rehabilitating the lawbreaker and bringing him back to society as a useful citizen. Someone has said that the usual prison program is really designed not to rehabilitate the prisoner but rather to prevent trouble within the prison. It is recognized by authorities that prisons basically are places in which to keep people locked up and removed from society, and that they can do little more than perform that basic function.
I should therefore like to suggest that in considering the new emphasis on reform and rehabilitation, we should give some attention to solutions to the problem other than the actual program conducted within the walls of the reformatory. This problem has been brought into focus in the last year. Since we last discussed these matters in this chamber there have been several outbreaks of

Supply-Justice
violence and rioting in some of our penal institutions in Canada. Last August, for example, we had the problem at Kingston penitentiary. Later on in my own province of Manitoba there was some difficulty at Stony Mountain penitentiary and later in our provincial jail at Headingley, and then in the local jail in my own city of Brandon, Manitoba.
An article relating to the rioting last August 15 at Kingston penitentiary appeared shortly thereafter, on October 15, in Maclean's magazine. It is supposed to have been written as a result of information provided by an ex-convict of that institution. There is one section of this article that I should like to put on the record, because I think it indicates the difficulty and the futility of trying to undertake rehabilitation and reform within the walls of the institution itself. Here is the description of a typical day or part of a day within the walls of Kingston penitentiary:
There is a large bell in the centre of the rotunda. A guard whams it with a hammer at 7.30 and you're out of bed. It is the first of a hundred bells you hear throughout the day as you shuffle through the dreary prison timetable of eating, working and playing. After dressing in brown denim pants, shirt, jacket and cap, and pulling on the army-style prison boots, you give your face a dab at the basin. You don't have to shave every morning; you may go a week if you wish. You fold your bed against the wall, pick up your tray and mug, still dirty from last night's supper, and stand at the cell door. Another bell sounds and the hack-
That is the prison vernacular for guard.
-in charge of your range unlocks the master lock for the whole range of cells. This moves a steel I-beam out of position at the top of the cell range, so that the vertical locking bolt on each door may be raised and the cell door opened.
And on and on it goes in that same vein, describing mechanical, routine, monotonous drudgery.
I was very much interested in noticing the use of the word "hack" in the story provided by the ex-convict because words such as "hack," "screw" or "dick" seem to be part of the general parlance of ex-convicts and express the hostility and the bitterness that arise as a result of incarceration within the penal institutions.
I should like to say just a few words on the other aspects of this problem of rehabilitation and reform, and they are aspects that have not been tried to any considerable extent in Canada. They are the programs of probation, parole and after-care. I wish to emphasize at the outset of these remarks that I am not suggesting the mollycoddling of our prisoners. There are many cases of criminality which obviously require severe punishment, and there are many types of
[Mr. Dinsdale.l
criminals; there is the incorrigible, the habitual or the recidivist. But there are large numbers-and they are actually the larger percentage of our so-called criminal population-who commit occasional offences due to special and transient reasons.
The difficulty with our program today is that all these cases-whether they result from recidivism or mental deficiency, or whether it is the case of a first and young offender- are treated very much after the same fashion. Canada has a parole system but, as I have indicated, it has not been used to any large extent; and it would seem to me, as a result of reading the report on the riot at Headingley jail, for example, that many prisoners are retained in our institutions beyond the point where institutional treatment serves any useful purpose either to the individual or to society.
It must always be remembered that there are two sides to this problem, namely the necessity of providing punishment or rehabilitation for the prisoner and at the same time protection for society. The report on the Headingley jail incident indicates that to a large extent there is no useful program of training or employment of any kind within the institution. In fact, in a recently constructed vocational training wing a large part-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not want to object to my hon. friend's remarks, but surely conditions in Headingley jail have nothing to do with the estimates we are considering. If he would offer some criticism of our system and help us out by suggestions I think it would be much more to the point.
I was going to suggest that perhaps closer co-ordination might be helpful. Would that be pertinent?
Go ahead.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I would suggest to the hon. member for Brandon-Souris that he would certainly be in order in advocating closer co-ordination. But, as in a case we had this afternoon, just because he is advocating that co-ordination I do not think he should spend too much time describing the actual conditions in an institution for which the Minister of Justice is not responsible. I think he will appreciate the difference.

Yes, Mr. Chairman. I understand the problem. I think I can move from the Headingley report without any further comments, other than to indicate that there is no representative of the federal remission service resident in eastern Ontario or in any of the three prairie provinces, although there

are two penitentiaries and a number of provincial jails located in that area. I was using the Headingley report to point out that in my opinion there is a real need for somebody representing the remission service of Canada resident in one of those provinces, preferably the province of Manitoba.
Conditions of crowding in the prison were excessive at the time of the riot. The prison was built to accommodate 275 prisoners, but at the time of the difficulty there were actually '380 prisoners within the institution. So I think there could be very much closer co-operation between the remission branch and the provinces within our institutions, both federal and provincial, where there have been difficulties in the past year, and the past months.
The other possibility of coping with the problem of the increasing criminal population in Canada is that of making use of the probation system. The system of probation is the most hopeful, because actually it keeps persons out of prison. That is the best kind of rehabilitation, that which keeps the offenders of younger years, the first offenders, free from the stigma of a term in prison, and keeps them within the framework of society so they can be assisted by all the community resources available to make a successful adjustment.
Again, in Canada we have not used the probation system to any great extent. It was extended first to juveniles; and then in 1921, as the result of an amendment to the Criminal Code, it became possible to extend the probation principle to adult offenders. As an example of the slow progress made in the last 32 years, I should like to place on record some statistics which indicate that Canada's position in this regard is quite unfavourable when compared with that of, for example, the United Kingdom. To carry on a successful probation system one needs probation officers and supervisory staff of all kinds. At the present time there are just 50 such officers for all Canada, as compared with hundreds of police officers whose task, of course, is essentially the apprehension of lawbreakers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Where did the hon. member get his figure of 50?
From the latest report of the Canadian Penal Association.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think it is quite wrong.
Is it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, I think so. I shall be referring to that, but I think the situation is much better than my hon. friend believes it is.
Supply-Justice
That is good.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If I remember correctly, the number is much greater than that for Ontario alone.

This is the latest report, dated 1953, and is taken from the proceedings of the meeting of the Canadian Penal Association on October 15 and 16, 1953. It is pointed out further in these statistics that 40 per cent of all crimes of violence in this country were committed by young offenders between the ages of 16 and 26. Again, it points out that 60 per cent of all offenders were committed to prison for periods of 90 days or less.
These are the categories that could benefit most from an extended system of probation and thus ease the pressure on our prison population. I feel-and there are many authorities in the field who support this viewpoint-that it would help to prevent the growing problem of recidivism if we were able to keep these younger offenders free entirely from the taint and stigma of prison incarceration. So I would urge very strongly that something be done to implement a more vigorous use of the principle of probation.
The need is growing from year to year. For example, in 1950 there were over 98,000 persons incarcerated in Canadian prisons while in the same year, with three times our population, the United Kingdom had less than 35,000 persons. That is 98,000 as compared with 35,000. In 1950 there were 3,631 adult offenders placed on probation in Canada, of which 2,075 were in Ontario, where there is a fairly advanced program of probation in operation. On the other hand, in the United Kingdom 34,000 adult offenders were placed on probation. That indicates a comparison of 3,000 to 34,000. It seems to me there is a very great opportunity for improvement along these lines.
Then there is the major difficulty which faces every Canadian who, as the result of an infraction of our laws, has been sent to a prison for a longer or shorter period of time, and that is the necessity of returning to society after his sentence has been served. The program I outlined very briefly from the report of the former inmate of Kingston penitentiary indicates that from a routine of that kind an institutional personality would tend to result, a personality that is out of touch with the world and, to a large extent, out of touch with reality.
The suggestion is made by those who have given attention to the problem, particularly in provincial institutions, that adjustments to society might be eased by making provision for home leaves, as is done in the old

Supply-J ustice
country, and also by reducing maximum care and substituting open-house or custodial care under which the prisoner has a reasonable degree of freedom, and where conditions are not too far removed from those he finds when eventually he returns to society.
The tragedy, in the case of all prisoners, is that punishment really begins following their discharge. The prisoner is stamped with the stigma of the ex-convict. In many cases police tend to hound him. If he has been engaged in professional or commercial positions requiring bonding by a bonding company, he cannot be bonded because of his prison record. In fact the finding of employment is one of the big problems of the exconvict. No private employer is willing to take the risk. Unfortunately the Canadian civil service will not give an opportunity to a discharged prisoner. This opens a wide area of discussion. It might be that the services of the federal employment offices could be utilized in helping prisoners make adjustment in suitable employment.
There is one oversight that has worked special hardship. The prisoner who is eligible for unemployment insurance is not able to obtain his benefits because of the regulation that he must have made contributions immediately prior to his application for the insurance. Of course his removal from society has made the meeting of those terms impossible.
In most cases the only money a discharged prisoner has to assist in his readjustment to society is an infinitesimally small discharge gratuity. It is the gratuity he has earned as the result of a per diem grant. The grant is so small that in most cases where there are no family resources behind the prisoner he returns to society practically insolvent. The suggestion is put forward that the rates of such gratuities should be based on need for survival

that is, maintaining the basic creature needs-rather than on the length of the sentence served.
In a good many cases the discharged prisoner, shunned by so-called respectable society because of the prison stigma, is reduced to the flop-house existence and to cast-off clothing. In too many cases he joins the ranks of our transients and vagrants, who in turn begin to swell the ranks of our habitual recidivist criminals. Unfortunately, too, as I indicated in my opening remarks, any beneficial effect that has resulted from the custodial care is completely lost because of the gap in our program of rehabilitation, which provides very little assistance in the very important problem of returning to society and finding a useful place there once again.
CMr. Dinsdale.]
I must say a word on the work of the voluntary agencies. Actually they are the only group who are trying to fill the tremendous need in this regard. I notice in the estimates that item 170 provides grants of $40,000 to recognized prisoners' aid societies, as may be approved by the treasury board. That is a beginning in the right direction. However, I think it will be agreed that $40,000, when compared with the rather substantial expenditures for custodial care, is hardly adequate to meet the after-care problem.
There is no easy solution to this difficulty. Of course grants could be increased to prisoners' aid associations such as the John Howard society, the Elizabeth Fry society, and the Salvation Army. It is true that many prisoners prefer to work through the private agencies, mainly because those private prisoners' aid societies are in contact with the prisoner throughout the entire period of incarceration and are planning for his reestablishment in society almost from the moment he is sentenced. Then again, if we are going to deal with the growing problem of crime, it is necessary to have a close partnership between government departments and private agencies. The rehabilitation of the lawbreaker requires the resources of all the community if he is to be brought back to a useful place in society.
I urgently request the minister to give some consideration to enlarging the activities provided under probation and parole for the solution of this very difficult problem.

Mr. Chairman, vote 170 is actually a very important one, though it involves only a few thousand dollars. It reads:
Administration of the office of the commissioner of penitentiaries, including $40,000 for grants to recognized prisoners' aid societies, as may be approved by the treasury board.
Actually the vote is therefore a policy vote on the operation of the penitentiaries and on the care after an inmate leaves the institution.
I am not going to hold up the committee this evening for any great length of time on the actual care inside the institution, because on more than one occasion I have spoken on these matters in the house. But I do want to draw the attention of the Minister of Justice to this fact. The minister is interested in penitentiary care and has established by royal commission or by appointment a board on several phases of institutional care and penology. I would appreciate it if the minister would give us some indication as to when he expects the

reports will be received on the various studies that are now being made under his authority.
So far as institutional care is concerned, there is just one aspect that I should like the minister to comment on, not as Minister of Justice but as a man. Since he makes the regulations, he must know something about those whom he is regulating.
Sir, I have been in this House of Commons only some two years, but I have had an interest in penology for some 22 years, not from an office desk but from meeting men and women in provincial and federal jails. I want to make this very clear, Mr. Chairman. We who make the law in parliament and those who enforce the law would be doing a disservice to society if we became sentimental about criminals. We must not at any time become sentimental toward criminals. We who make or enforce the law must not at any time coddle those who have broken the law.
Having expressed that as my opinion, that you must not be sentimental, you must not coddle those who break the law, I do maintain that it is our responsibility to try to rehabilitate those who are anti-social and who are in our institutions. I do not believe it can be done under some of the conditions we find in our provincial jails and federal penitentiaries today.
Perhaps I personally am sentimental. If so I have no apologies to make. A letter from the family means a great deal. A visit from a member of the family means a great deal. I cannot understand why the Minister of Justice, who has the administration of the penitentiaries of Canada, should still insist upon the limitation of three letters a month, which I understand has now been increased by one. I am keeping complete track of the regulations, and I know it has been increased by one.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

Would it not be good psychiatry, good psychology, good humanitarianism and benevolence; would it not help to rehabilitate these men who have broken the law and who are paying the penalty if they were allowed contact with their families? While the minister is talking to his deputies would he ask them why it is that a man who has lived with a common-law wife for 12 years, who has had four children by that common-law wife, should not be permitted to have her visit him in the penitentiary? I know we have great respect for marriage, but I hope we have greater respect for love.

Oh, oh.
Supply-Justice

Don't laugh. Unfortunately at times there is a difference between love and marriage. If a man is in love and lives with a common-law wife for 12 years; if he has no right to marry her legally and has children by her; if he breaks the law and is sent to the penitentiary, why should there be so much trouble in getting permission for her to visit him in the penitentiary?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows, but the rest of the members of the committee do not know, just what the regulation is. Regulation 16-A-2 reads:
When an inmate has lived in a common law relationship prior to incarceration and satisfactory evidence is produced to the warden that
(i)	the relationship has existed for a period of at least one year and during such period the inmate has supported and publicly represented the person with whom he has been living as his wife
(ii)	there is mutual intent to resume relationship upon release
(iii)	neither party has a legal spouse who has notified the warden that he or she objects to such visits and correspondence being authorized, the warden may grant to such inmate the privilege of visits and correspondence with the common-law partner in accordance with the provisions of these regulations.
The minister has read the regulation correctly, but he has forgotten something-if they do not have a legal spouse.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: A legal spouse who objects. Surely the legal spouse has some rights in the picture.

There are some cases where a man and woman have been separated because under our antiquated divorce laws you cannot get a divorce except on the ground of adultery. There are a lot of people in Canada who are living in legal immorality because they cannot be divorced under our antiquated divorce laws. I have in mind this case where a man lived with his common-law wife for 12 years. She is now being allowed to visit her husband in the penitentiary, but why should a person have to go through all these trials and tribulations? Why should she have to get in touch with her member of parliament and carry on correspondence back and forth in order to have the right to visit that man in the penitentiary? I think a new approach is required to this matter. It should not require a board or a royal commission to decide how many letters or how many visits should be granted to an inmate.
The major point I wish to raise under this item is the treatment given to inmates after discharge. I find it just a little bit difficult to speak at times because everybody knows of my interest in this matter. Some may think I am sentimental about it, but I am

Supply-Justice
not. I want to try to save lives; I want to try to save people; I want to try to save the taxpayers' money.
I think we are making a big mistake in this country because we have not recognized that after we sentence people to from two years to life in a penitentiary and then release them, the taxpayer has a big investment in them. We have had to pay to get those people into jail. We have had to pay in order to train them. Then they are released at the termination of their sentences, and what do we do with them? Do we help them? Do we rehabilitate them? Do we try to make sure they do not break the law again? After an experience of over 22 years, during which time I have talked to people in the provincial jails and in the penitentiaries, I have come to the conclusion that immediately they get outside the doors of the jail they are on their own; nothing is done for them outside of giving them a new suit of clothes and $10 in their pocket.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am sure my hon. friend knows perfectly well that they are not on their own if they want any help, and a great many of them do want help. If I have the time tonight I will be glad to put on the record the numbers who have been helped, and they run into the hundreds. The total of those on ticket of leave is in the hundreds at any one time. It is hardly fair for my hon. friend to say what he is saying, that they do not have any help, that they are left to shift on their own resources.
I did not say they did not have any help.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They have all the help they want.
No, they do not.
Oh, oh.

No, they do not. Mr. Chairman, through you I say they do not. I am not talking just as one who sits here in the House of Commons opposite the Minister of Justice. I am talking as one who has had to deal with these men day after day and year after year. I say there is no policy provincially or federally-I am going to refer only to the matter from the federal angle-of taking care of men and women once they are released from the penitentiary, and rehabilitating them on a substantial basis. I say most definitely and from personal knowledge that we have no policy in Canada to take care of people once they are out of the penitentiary.
I say it would be a marvellous investment if we gave more attention to that issue. Yes,
I know that in British Columbia a man can be released. But where can he go? To the 
John Howard society. For what? A job? A handout? Yes. Help? Yes. But is there any follow-up care? No, sir. Don't try to kid me, because you cannot do so. We have not a follow-up care in Canada after a man's release from jail. Partially, yes; I agree. I give every thanks for the work that is being done. I give every thanks for the money that is now being expended. But because of the investment of Canada in those whom we keep in jail and train in jail, I say without any hesitation whatsoever that we are not taking advantage of the opportunity to rehabilitate these people. That is what I have been told time after time after time by those with whom I have conferred in the provincial jails and in our penitentiaries. I have asked, "What is your big problem?" They reply, "When they go out of here they say: Where do we go and who is interested in us?"

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I wonder whether my hon. friend is aware, for example, that in 1954- and that is fairly recently-there were 915 tickets of leave, of whom 576 had supervision by trained social workers or representatives of the remission service. Would he not regard that as being of some assistance? What more assistance would he suggest that we provide for them, other than putting them on a pension or something of that sort?

My hon. friend is not going to put me in that spot, Mr. Chairman. Pension? No. But I say we have not a follow-up service in Canada that we should have, or a rehabilitation service that we should have.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There were 576 in one year under supervision. Is that not a fairly good record, with 576 under the supervision of a trained social worker or a representative of the remission service?
Out of how many that were discharged? How many were discharged that year?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There were 915 discharged that year.
Where?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In the whole service and in all penitentiaries. Out of 915, 225 had only police supervision, which I know my hon. friend would regard as unsatisfactory. But 576 had supervision of trained social workers or representatives of the remission service.
I think that is not a bad record at all.
Where did you put them?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Put whom?
They were under supervision, but not under allocation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am saying that 576 were under supervision by trained social workers. That is not to say they stood there 10 hours a day watching what they did. But you know how these case workers operate. They have a certain number, not more than they can supervise properly. They advise and secure positions for them through the employment service, and help them in every way possible. I would say that 576 out of 915 discharged in that year under ticket of leave-
How many would be employed?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I could get that figure; I do not have it, but a large number would be employed.
Those are on ticket of leave.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

I know this business of parole and ticket of leave. But, of all those discharged from the penitentiary system of Canada, how many come under that? I maintain that in view of the money we have to spend in keeping these men in jail and training them in jail, the people of Canada might be able to stop a number of those men from going back into crime if we had a better follow-up service on those who are coming out of jail.
Mr. Chairman, I have seen and spoken to so many coming out of jail. I have asked, "What are you going to do?" They answered two things; one, "I am going to get drunk", and two, "I have some other thought in mind." You know what that is-a woman. Then they have to find jobs. They have no unemployment insurance. I am not being sentimental. I am interested in the rehabilitation of these people. I shall say no more, except that I think we need a greater program of follow-through on the people whom we have paid to keep in the penitentiary system of Canada. It will pay good dividends if we do not drop our responsibility when they have served their sentence, but carry it through for a longer time.

Mr. Chairman, a year ago we called the minister's attention to a 13-year-old lad in a penitentiary. I must be correct and admit that he was in a training school attached to the penitentiary. In the course of our discussion of that case it was revealed that there were in various parts of Canada a goodly number of lads aged from 13 to 16 in the various penitentiaries. I hope the minister at this time is able to inform the house that this condition no longer exists,
Supply-J ustice
that some remedy has since been found. I know the difficulties of the minister in connection with this, as he so well pointed out a year ago.
It is rather odd that Canadians as Canadians have a series of duties and responsibilities which they must fulfil, but when it comes to the rights of Canadians as citizens, we have rights as Canadians only in so far as the 10 provincial attorneys general choose to grant us those rights. If the minister is unable to report to the house that this matter is being taken care of-I see the minister nodding his head, so I shall rest for a moment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am very happy to announce that I received a report on this young man on June 24. It was to the effect that he has got along very well. His conduct has been good and he has been attending school regularly, and since last November he has been undergoing vocational training in the bricklaying trade, in which he has made good progress. He has now been released under the supervision of a charitable organization where we think he will continue to make good progress.

May I follow through and ask the minister whether any progress is being made in persuading local law enforcement officers, or whoever is responsible, to see to it that fewer and fewer of these younger people are sent to the penitentiaries? Is any headway being made? I understand that at most points in Canada this situation could not arise. I hope the day is not far distant when no boy anywhere in Canada can be sentenced to penitentiary. Has any progress been made toward having more areas in Canada meet this desirable condition?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think it would be fair to say some progress has been made, but a good deal of the difficulty, as in this young lad's case, is that we had facilities with which we could help him and which were not available elsewhere. While I am not advocating for one moment that lads of his age should go to the penitentiary, still I think in his case he is better off for having gone there. It will not be until the same facilities can be provided in provincial institutions that we will not get the odd young lad like that in the penitentiaries. I think it is rather revealing that when they do go to our penitentiaries, pretty good results are usually achieved.

I appreciate the report the minister is making and I agree with most of what he says. However, I believe he will agree with me that another type of institution would be more desirable for youngsters

Supply-Justice
of that age. Has the minister given consideration at any time to establishing a national institution under his jurisdiction or under the jurisdiction of the chief commissioner of penitentiaries to which all such cases could be assigned, rather than have possibly hundreds of youngsters suffer until the local authorities in some isolated areas of Canada provide the necessary facilities? Is it the case that the numbers are not enough to warrant the establishment of a separate institution?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think it would be very much more desirable on almost every count that offenders of that age should be taken care of under provincial auspices. Not only do I think that is so, but I think in the long run very much better results would be obtained by their being so taken care of. I do not think we have any reason to despair as to the possibility of that at all.

I visited the penitentiary with the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam when this young lad was there. The minister will recall that the hon. member placed quite a damaging report on Hansard with respect to this young lad, and that I suggested that the minister communicate with his officers because I was sure he would get quite a different picture. I gather the report he has now given is a report from his officers.
I quite agree with the minister that this 13-year-old boy has had in a federal penitentiary, for the first time in his life, the experience of having teachers and friends who were sympathetic and anxious to give the boy a lift in life. I feel sure that the prediction the minister is making now will be realized and that this young lad, as the result of association with well trained personnel in the federal training department connected with St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary, will be a worth-while citizen.

When the estimates of the Department of Justice were up before I made some remarks with regard to the relative conditions that we find in our own country and in Britain. I have some material here I should like to put on the record, not at any great length but it will take more than two or three minutes and I do not know whether it is sensible to begin now. I think I would want about 10 minutes. I shall begin now, if the committee wishes; otherwise, as it is three minutes to ten-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: May I point out to the committee that there are only three items left in the main estimates of this department and four in the supplementaries. Is it the unanimous view of the committee that we should sit until this department is concluded?
Agreed.
Mr. Chairman, I did not quite get what you said. Are we going to sit until we finish the department?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Until we finish this department.
I did not agree to that.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I have no desire-
I certainly do not want to feel that anything I have to say is keeping people here to their discomfort after ten o'clock. I will not agree with that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think I know the figures my hon. friend has because I have looked at the same book, "Canadian Welfare", and actually the figures are not very accurate. I think if the hon. member and I got together I could convince him that was the case.
So far as his general thesis is concerned, I thought when he made his remarks on the last occasion, if he will permit me to say so, he opened up what is probably the most important subject matter in the Department of Justice at the present time. It was touched on again tonight by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris. The subject matter is how we are going to save for society, to put the matter at the beginning on a very low basis, a lot of needless cost in keeping people incarcerated in prisons and penitentiaries when we could avoid doing that, I think, by reform in the practices we have been following in the past. I am entirely in agreement with what I take to be the hon. member's viewpoint in that regard.

The minister has confirmed me in my feeling that this matter should not be dealt with casually in a few minutes. I think it is of tremendous importance, and he himself has also said so. I think that prima facie it raises a question that every member of the house ought to regard as what shall I say-a challenge. The figures given are so disturbing.
In the last two weeks I have also learned something further about the matter which I perhaps should have known before and which I doubt if everyone in the house knows. If the minister had said that this was a trivial matter and we had better just let it go, I might have doubted my own judgment. I do not like to be disagreeable and disobliging, but I think this is an important matter. I certainly want to have my doubts and discomforts about the matter answered, and I cannot believe that anything that could take place in 10 or 15 minutes would make me feel they had been answered.
We have the recommendation of the Archambault commission with regard to the

question of probation. I have here a statement by Lord Samuel giving the most astounding figures with respect to England. They show that in 30 years convictions in England have gone down from 180,000 to 34,000. It is almost incredible. There may be explanations, but here is a statement by Lord Samuel showing that there has been a reduction in the figures in the period from 1907 to 1937 from 180,000 to 60,000. Then the writer of the article, who is a competent man, has this to say:
Had Lord Samuel been speaking in 1950 he would have been able to state a further reduction of one-half in the number of people committed to prison in England and Wales-34,825.
As I understand it, what almost seems like a miracle has come about largely through the effects of probation. As I understand the situation in Canada, unless something has happened in the last year or two we have made only the first beginnings, and we are faced with the fact, which I could not believe at first but which apparently is true, that we are still having nearly 10 times as many convictions proportionately.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is quite wrong.
Here is the last figure.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend is misinterpreting the figures.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
And in addition, they are
inaccurate.
I have not misinterpreted the figures. These figures go up to 1950. Their population, as the minister knows, is about three times as great, and-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If we are going to go on and debate the matter, I think it would be desirable, in the interests of a proper understanding on the part of the Canadian people of what are the facts, that all the facts should be accurately stated.
So do I.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My suggestion was going to be this. There is nothing new about this problem. We have been conscious of this problem for a long while in the Department of Justice. But as my friend the hon. member for Greenwood is aware-

May I interrupt the
minister for one moment? I promise not to do it again. I interrupt in order to make it clear that I was not aware of it. I have spoken to other members in the house who were just as ignorant as I was. I therefore think the minister is wrong in saying that this is an old problem and that we are all
Supply-Justice
aware of it. I do not think we are aware of it. Certainly that is so unless I have chosen entirely untypical members of this house to speak to. We are not aware of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I cannot speak for any person but myself and my officials but we have been aware of it. We have had a system of remission in the Department of Justice under which we have released many hundreds of persons under ticket of leave, and under which we have released all that we thought we could safely release. That is a federal function, a federal responsibility, under our divided system which does not obtain in those jurisdictions of which my friend the hon. member for Greenwood is thinking. In Europe where they have a unitary government'-in Belgium, Holland, England and these other places-they do not have the problem of divided jurisdiction that we have under a federal system. Under our federal system, however, the provision for probation, the thing that is worrying my hon. friend from Greenwood, has to be made by the provinces.
I realize that fact fully.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is the important thing. With a view to providing the foundation upon which we could reasonably call the provinces together in a dominion-provincial conference to discuss this matter we-as I think every hon. member of this committee is aware- appointed an advisory committee under Mr. Justice Fauteux of the Supreme Court of Canada and made up of himself, Mr. W. B. Common, Q.C., director of public prosecutions for the province of Ontario; Mr. J. Alex Edmison, Q.C., assistant to the principal at Queen's University and former president of the Canadian Penal Association; and Mr. Joseph McCulley, who is now warden of Hart House at the University of Toronto and for some years was a valued assistant commissioner of penitentiaries at Ottawa. We thought that if we could get a report, which we expect to receive about October of this year, we would then have a mass of data which we could place before the provinces- in a matter which is their business and not ours and in which we have no overriding control over them at all but can only inspire action by persuasion-upon the strength of which we could carry on an intelligent discussion in the dominion-provincial conference with the hope-and so far as I am concerned, the confident hope-that we could get all the provinces at the same time to instal a system of probation across Canada. So far as I can see, that is the only way in which we can get it.

Supply-Justice
This is not going to be as difficult as one might expect. The hon. member for Brandon-Souris said that there were 50 probation officers, I believe, in the whole of Canada. The facts are that the province of Ontario already has, I would say, a good probation system in actual operation. At the present time they have 78 full-time probation officers working in that province alone.
Are those probation officers dealing with adult offenders or juvenile offenders?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think all offenders.
I meant adult offenders.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The commissioner of penitentiaries tells me these Ontario probation officers deal with adult offenders.
This is a most important discussion, and it should not be closed up hurriedly. Would the minister call it ten o'clock?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The point I am getting at is this. I have no objection to adjourning. I am not anxious for the few remaining justice estimates to be rushed through hurriedly. However we can talk about this matter of probation as much as we like, but the fact of the matter is that there is not much likelihood of action at the provincial level until we can get the report of this advisory committee which was appointed for that express purpose of gathering together suitable material to discuss. Until we have that material to lay before the provinces we are not likely to make much progress with them. In the meanwhile we can debate it here but we shall be talking pro and con without producing too many tangible results.
My suggestion that I thought might reasonably be laid before the committee was that we might pass the estimates of the Department of Justice tonight. Then when we get this report this fall, we would bring it with this matter before the house at the next session. In the meanwhile I would hope that on the basis of that report we could call the attorneys general of the provinces together and discuss the whole problem which, as the hon. member for Greenwood rightly says, is a most important problem indeed. No matter how much we may disagree about statistics, I think that the hon. member for Greenwood and I will be in complete agreement that what they have been able to achieve in Great Britain and in other countries has been the product to a very large degree indeed of a system of probation under which a man who has committed an offence does not go behind prison walls at all. He 
stays out on probation. He does not become a statistic. He does not become a convict. Where we are not dealing with a mere theory but with a practice which has, in fact, in many of these other countries, produced the most excellent results, I cannot see, from my own point of view, why we cannot duplicate those results in Canada if we can get all the provinces to agree to do so. But I do believe, as I pointed out to my hon. friend, that to attempt to do that before we have a complete and comprehensive report from a competent body would be a mistake.
May I make one comment?
Let us call it ten o'clock.

I want to make one comment on what the minister has said. I think it is a great pity that this matter has not been discussed before. I certainly blame myself for my ignorance, and there may be others who feel the same way I do. I think the half hour, hour or whatever time is necessary to be spent in discussing this subject would be well worth while, because I may say quite frankly that I am inclined to think that the minister was passing this off too lightly-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Passing it off too lightly? Why
did we appoint this advisory committee under Mr. Justice Fauteux?
Let me finish. I say he was passing it off too lightly in asking us to rush these things through after ten o'clock on Friday night. I do not consider that should be done.
Ten o'clock.

There are matters that have not been referred to a royal commission, or points that come under the penitentiaries administration, that I personally should like to discuss and I think they are important. I would therefore ask that we call it ten o'clock.
